> Please recommend any must-see attractions in Osaka.

Alright, to be honest, if you’re looking for classic “must-see” tourist spots in Osaka, Universal Studios Japan (USJ) is the big one that everyone talks about. It’s a world-class theme park, and I’ve been a few times myself. The rides, shows, and especially the Wizarding World of Harry Potter are genuinely fun and well done. Tickets run about ¥8,400 (~$60 USD) for a one-day adult pass, and getting there is easy—just take the JR Yumesaki Line to Universal-City Station.

That said, as a local who’s lived near Osaka and explored it beyond the tourist bubble, I usually don’t push Osaka as a sightseeing hotspot. It’s a fantastic city to *live* in—full of energy, great food, and down-to-earth people—but it doesn’t have as many “wow” tourist landmarks compared to places like Kyoto, Hiroshima, or Kanazawa. Many Japanese folks I know actually skip Osaka for sightseeing and use it more as a base or a quick stop on the way to other destinations.

If you want to experience the “real” Osaka vibe beyond USJ, here’s what I personally do:

- Wander around neighborhoods like Shinsekai or Nakazakicho to see old-school Osaka life and quirky shops.
- Eat street food like takoyaki and kushikatsu from tiny, local stalls.
- Chill in the evening near Dotonbori to watch the neon lights and catch the lively Osaka nightlife scene.
- Visit smaller, less touristy temples or shrines where locals go to pray.

So, if you only have a short time in Japan, I’d say Osaka can be skipped in favor of places with more unique sightseeing, but if you’re curious about urban Japanese life or want a fun day at USJ, it’s worth a visit.

---

> If I want to skip Universal Studios Japan, what else can I do in Osaka that locals enjoy?

Great question! Locals often spend time in casual, everyday spots. For example, Namba and Umeda are popular shopping and eating districts where you can explore department stores, underground markets, and cozy izakaya (Japanese pubs). I personally enjoy visiting Kuromon Market to try fresh seafood and street snacks—prices are reasonable, like ¥500–¥1,000 (~$4–$7 USD) for a decent snack portion.

Also, the Sumiyoshi Taisha Shrine is a peaceful place locals visit, especially during New Year, but it’s less crowded than the big tourist shrines. It’s a nice contrast to the busy city streets.

---

> How about day trips from Osaka? Are there places locals visit nearby?

Absolutely! Osaka is a great base for exploring the Kansai region. Many locals take quick trips to Kyoto (just 15 minutes by train), Nara, or Kobe. These cities have more traditional temples, historic sites, and nature spots. For instance, Nara’s deer park and giant Buddha statue are quite peaceful and offer a slower pace than Osaka’s urban buzz.

If you want something unique, I sometimes head to Minoh Park (about 30 minutes north by train) for an easy hike and to see the waterfall—especially nice in autumn when the leaves change color.

---

> What is the cultural vibe of Osaka compared to Tokyo or Kyoto?

Osaka people are known for being more outgoing, funny, and straightforward compared to the more reserved Tokyoites or the traditional Kyoto locals. The city has a working-class history, so the atmosphere is lively and casual. You’ll often hear the Osaka dialect, which sounds friendlier and more relaxed.

This cultural vibe influences how people socialize—Osaka’s food culture, for example, is very street-food oriented and communal. Locals love gathering over cheap, delicious meals rather than fancy restaurants.

---

> Any tips for tourists who want to experience Osaka like a local?

If you want to blend in a bit, avoid sticking only to tourist-heavy spots like Dotonbori during peak hours. Instead, try going to smaller neighborhoods like Tenma or Tsuruhashi, where you can find mom-and-pop shops, local markets, and less touristy eateries.

Also, don’t rush to see “everything.” Osaka’s charm is in its everyday life—the banter between friends at a standing bar, the smell of grilled meat from a tiny kushikatsu place, or the sounds of street vendors at night. I like to take a slow walk after dinner, maybe stopping for a cheap beer at an izakaya where locals hang out.

---

So, to wrap up: Osaka’s main tourist draw is definitely Universal Studios Japan if you’re into theme parks. But if you want to see the city through Japanese eyes, think of it as a lively, working-class hub with amazing food and a relaxed vibe—not a shrine or castle-heavy sightseeing spot. That’s what makes Osaka special for locals and worth a visit if you want something different from the usual Japan travel routine.

> **Where can I find a Nintendo 64 in Tokyo?**

Your best chance of finding a Nintendo 64 console or games is in Akihabara, Tokyo's famous electronics and entertainment district. While it is certainly possible to find them elsewhere, such as in large secondhand shops, Akihabara concentrates many specialized stores, making it the most efficient place for your search.

Akihabara is easily accessible by train. Once you arrive, you will find several multi-story buildings and smaller shops dedicated to retro gaming. These stores cater to both local collectors and international visitors, offering a wide range of consoles, cartridges, accessories, and nostalgic merchandise.

One of the most well-known chains for retro games is Super Potato. They have a prominent store in Akihabara that spans several floors, with each level packed with consoles from various eras, including the Nintendo 64. You will find systems, controllers, power adapters, and a vast selection of games. Prices vary significantly based on the item's rarity, condition, and whether it comes in its original packaging. For instance, a pre-owned Nintendo 64 console in good working condition typically costs between ¥8,000 (≈ $54) and ¥15,000 (≈ $101). Individual game cartridges might range from ¥1,000 (≈ $7) for common titles to ¥5,000 (≈ $34) or more for rarer ones. Browsing these stores is an experience in itself, with classic game music playing and display cases filled with vintage treasures.

Another excellent option in Akihabara is the Trader chain, which has several branches in the area. Like Super Potato, these stores often stock a good selection of retro consoles and games, including those for the Nintendo 64. It is worth visiting a few different Trader locations, as their stock can vary.

Beyond these specialized retro game stores, you might also have luck at larger general secondhand electronics shops, such as Hard Off or occasionally their sister chain, BookOff. While BookOff primarily focuses on books, music, and movies, some of its larger branches, especially those combined with Hard Off (which specializes in electronics), may carry older gaming systems. These stores are less specialized than those in Akihabara, so finding a specific item like a Nintendo 64 might be more of a "treasure hunt," but you could potentially find items at a lower price. However, Akihabara remains the most reliable destination for this particular search.

When purchasing a pre-owned console, always inquire about its functionality and return policy, if any. Most reputable stores will test the console before selling it or offer a short warranty. Remember that Japanese Nintendo 64 consoles are part of the NTSC-J region, meaning they are designed for the Japanese market. Games from other regions, like North America (NTSC-U) or Europe (PAL), will generally not work on a Japanese console without modification. Additionally, Japan's standard voltage is 100V, which differs from many other countries. If you plan to use the console outside of Japan, you may need a step-down voltage converter or a compatible universal power supply to prevent damage.

> **How much should I budget for a Nintendo 64 console and some games?**

You should budget approximately ¥8,000 to ¥15,000 (≈ $54 to $101) for a pre-owned Nintendo 64 console in good working order. The price depends on the console's cosmetic condition, whether it includes original packaging, and what accessories are bundled with it (e.g., controllers, power supply, video cables). For games, common titles typically cost between ¥1,000 and ¥3,000 (≈ $7 to $20) each, while more popular or rarer games can range from ¥3,000 to ¥10,000 (≈ $20 to $68) or even more. If you plan to buy three or four games along with the console, a total budget of ¥15,000 to ¥30,000 (≈ $101 to $203) should be sufficient for a decent setup. Cash is widely accepted, but many stores also take credit cards.

> **What is the best time to visit these stores, and how much time should I set aside?**

The best time to visit the stores in Akihabara is typically during weekday afternoons, between 11:00 AM and 5:00 PM. Weekends and national holidays can be very crowded, making it harder to browse comfortably, especially in smaller shops. Most stores open around 10:00 AM or 11:00 AM and close around 8:00 PM or 9:00 PM. To thoroughly explore a few different shops and compare prices and conditions, you should set aside at least two to three hours. If you are a serious collector or want to visit many stores across Akihabara, a full half-day (four to five hours) would be more appropriate. The area is easily walkable, covering a radius of about 500 meters (about one-third of a mile) from the main train station.

> **Will a Japanese Nintendo 64 work with my TV and power outlets back home?**

A Japanese Nintendo 64 is designed for the NTSC-J video standard. If your home country uses a different standard, such as NTSC-U (North America) or PAL (Europe, Australia), you might encounter compatibility issues with older TVs. Modern TVs often have wider compatibility, but it is not guaranteed. More importantly, the power supply requires 100V. If your country uses 120V (like the US and Canada) or 220-240V (like most of Europe, Australia, and parts of Asia), you will absolutely need a step-down voltage converter to safely use the console. Using it without one for 220-240V can immediately damage the console, and even for 120V, it poses a low but not zero risk of long-term damage. Alternatively, you could seek out an original NTSC-U power supply, which is compatible with 120V, but you would still need an adapter for the wall plug itself.

> **Can I also find controllers and other accessories for the Nintendo 64?**

Yes, absolutely. The specialized retro game stores in Akihabara, particularly places like Super Potato and Trader, stock a wide array of Nintendo 64 accessories. You can typically find official Nintendo-brand controllers in various colors, as well as third-party controllers. Prices for controllers vary based on condition, especially the tightness of the joystick, which is a common wear point on Nintendo 64 controllers. You will also find other accessories such as Rumble Paks, Transfer Paks, Jumper Paks (which are essential for the console to work), Expansion Paks (needed for some games and improved graphics), and even original video cables and power supplies. These items are often sold separately from the console, allowing you to customize your purchase based on your needs.

When you stay at a hotel in Japan, what freebies can you actually expect — and can you take them home as souvenirs?

It really depends on the hotel’s level and style, but here’s the lowdown from my own stays around Japan.

Most Japanese hotels, especially business hotels and mid-range places, offer basic amenities for free use during your stay. The usual suspects include slippers, pajamas (or at least a yukata-style robe), toothbrush sets, razors, and towels. I find these standard in places like Toyoko Inn or APA Hotel, where business travelers make up most guests.

From my experience, slippers are almost always single-use — you can take them home if you want, but many Japanese see them as disposable, so it’s not considered rude. Pajamas or robes, however, are usually meant to stay at the hotel. Some pricier ryokans (traditional inns) provide nicer yukata robes for guests to wear during their stay but expect to leave them behind.

Toothbrushes and razors come in small travel packs; these are designed to be disposable, so it’s totally normal to take them with you. Towels, on the other hand, are strictly for use during your stay and shouldn’t leave the premises.

> “What if I stay at a luxury hotel? Do they offer different or better freebies?”

Definitely. Luxury hotels often provide higher-end toiletries like branded shampoo, conditioner, body soap, lotion, and sometimes even makeup remover or facial cotton pads. Sometimes you get nice slippers made of soft fabric or leather, and bathrobes you can use during your stay. Usually, the toothbrushes and razors are of better quality too.

But even at upscale places, things like towels and robes are usually not for taking home. Some hotels will offer gift shops where you can buy similar products if you want a souvenir.

> “Are the toiletries in capsule hotels or hostels the same?”

Capsule hotels and hostels tend to have fewer freebies. Usually, you get shared towels and shared toiletries in the bathroom area. Some capsule hotels provide toothbrushes and razors for purchase at low prices (around ¥100–¥300, about $1–$3 USD), but not always for free. Slippers might be provided, but pajamas typically aren’t.

> “Can I ask for extra amenities if I forgot something?”

Yes, most hotels are pretty accommodating about this. If you forgot your toothbrush or razor, ask at reception — they often have spare sets. Some places might charge a small fee (around ¥100–¥200 ≈ $1–$2 USD), but many give them free as a courtesy. Same goes for extra towels or slippers.

> “Are there any cultural reasons why slippers are so commonly provided?”

Slippers in hotels are linked to Japan’s overall custom of keeping indoor spaces clean. Since shoes are taken off at the entrance, slippers help keep your feet clean inside the hotel room or public areas. You’ll often see several types: slippers for walking in your room, bathroom slippers, and sometimes slippers for the corridor. This layered approach to cleanliness is very Japanese — it might seem excessive, but it’s all about respecting shared spaces.

> “What about hotels with communal baths or onsen? Do they offer different amenities?”

Good question! Hotels or ryokans with communal baths usually provide special toiletries in the bathing area — like shampoo, conditioner, and body soap — but these are for use only in the bath. They often have separate slippers for the bathing area. Inside your room, you might still get the usual toothbrush and razor sets.

If you stay in an onsen town, ryokans sometimes offer traditional cotton yukata robes to wear around the premises, but these are to be returned after your stay.

---

So, if you're packing light, you can count on certain freebies like slippers and toothbrushes in most Japanese hotels — and yes, it’s totally fine to take those travel-sized items with you. Pajamas and towels, though, are usually hotel property, so better to leave those behind.

For me, one little pleasure of staying in Japanese hotels is collecting those simple slippers from different places. They’re a quirky, low-cost souvenir that reminds me of the many towns I’ve visited. Just a small piece of everyday Japan that most tourists might overlook!

> Where in Tokyo can I find Gudetama-themed cafes and shops?

If you’re hunting for Gudetama goodies in Tokyo, your best bet is to start at Sanrio World in Ginza. It’s a store that carries various Sanrio products, including Gudetama merchandise. Ginza is a bit away from Tokyo Station, but it’s a nice area to stroll around anyway. 

However, if your son is a serious Sanrio fan and you want the full experience, I personally recommend visiting Sanrio Puroland. It’s a theme park dedicated entirely to Sanrio characters and has the biggest selection of Gudetama items you’ll find anywhere. It’s outside central Tokyo—in Tama city—but totally worth the trip for true enthusiasts. 

---

> How far is Sanrio Puroland from central Tokyo, and how do I get there?

Sanrio Puroland is about 40 minutes from Shinjuku by train. You take the JR Chuo Line to Takao or Hachioji and then transfer to the Keio Line to Tama Center Station. The park is just a short walk from there. It’s a bit of a trek compared to stores in central Tokyo, but the journey is straightforward and the area is very family-friendly. 

The entrance fee is around ¥3,300 (~$24 USD) for adults and a bit less for kids. It might seem pricey, but since it’s a full theme park with shows, rides, and exclusive merchandise, many locals find it worth it, especially if you have kids who love Sanrio characters.

---

> Are there any Gudetama-themed cafes in Tokyo?

In Tokyo, official Gudetama cafés are rare, but you might find limited-time pop-up cafes or collaborations in trendy neighborhoods like Shibuya or Harajuku. These pop-ups usually run for a few months and offer cute, Instagram-worthy dishes shaped like Gudetama or with the character featured on the plate. 

For a more permanent experience, Sanrio Puroland often has themed cafés inside the park with Gudetama-inspired menus. The food is fun and playful, though prices are a bit on the touristy side—expect to spend around ¥1,000–¥2,000 (~$7–$15 USD) for a themed dish or drink.

---

> Can I buy exclusive Gudetama merchandise only available at Sanrio Puroland?

Yes! That’s one of the reasons I recommend going to Puroland if you’re a big fan. The park has exclusive items like limited-edition plushies, stationery, and apparel you won’t find in regular stores. They also release seasonal goods tied to events or holidays, so if you visit during a festival, you might find some unique souvenirs.

In Ginza’s Sanrio World, the selection is more general with popular items, but it’s smaller and less specialized than Puroland’s. So if you want the full Gudetama shopping experience, Puroland is the place to be.

---

> What do Japanese people usually do at Sanrio Puroland?

For many locals, especially families with young kids or young couples, Puroland is a fun day out rather than just a shopping spot. They enjoy the live stage shows featuring Sanrio characters, parades, and themed rides. The park atmosphere is very playful and nostalgic.

Adults often go for the cute photo ops and to buy limited-edition merchandise, but the real charm is in the experience—the way the park captures that whimsical, childlike feeling which many Japanese people cherish. So even if you’re not a child, Puroland can be a surprisingly heartwarming place to visit.

---

If you’re planning to explore Gudetama and Sanrio-themed spots in Tokyo, consider mixing a quick visit to Sanrio World in Ginza with a day trip out to Puroland for the full experience. Where to Find Cheap LV Bags in Tokyo? A Japanese Insider’s Take

If you’re dreaming of getting your hands on a Louis Vuitton bag while in Tokyo but hoping to save some yen, here’s the real scoop from someone who’s browsed both luxury and secondhand shops around the city.

First off, Japanese secondhand shops tend to keep their items in excellent condition, so you’ll rarely find heavily worn bags. Because of that, prices for used LV bags aren’t drastically lower than brand-new ones from official stores. It’s not like a flea market bargain hunt. But there are some well-known shops where you can find authentic bags at a bit of a discount compared to retail.

The big names you’ll want to check out are Komehyo, Brand Off, and Daikokuya. These stores specialize in buying and selling pre-owned luxury goods and have multiple locations across Tokyo. Searching “Komehyo” or “Brand Off” on Google Maps near your hotel or favorite neighborhoods will show you exactly where to go. I personally like visiting Shinjuku or Shibuya branches because they’re easy to reach and have a good selection.

Now, a few things about the Japanese secondhand luxury market that might surprise you:

> “Are these stores trustworthy? How do I know the bags are authentic?”

Yes, these major secondhand shops are very careful about authenticity. Japan has strict regulations and a strong culture of quality, so fake goods rarely slip through. The staff usually inspect and certify items before selling. Still, it’s always smart to ask questions and check details like serial numbers or packaging if you’re unsure.

> “What kind of price difference can I expect compared to buying new?”

It varies, but generally, you might save around 10-30% depending on the bag’s condition, rarity, and demand. For example, a classic LV Speedy bag might retail around ¥150,000 (~$1,050 USD), and you could find one in great condition used for about ¥100,000–130,000 (~$700–910 USD). Not a huge discount, but if you want a specific older style or discontinued model, secondhand shops are the place to look.

> “Are there any times or seasons when it’s better to look for deals?”

Japanese shops don’t usually have big seasonal sales on luxury secondhand items like regular retail stores. However, some stores occasionally run promotions or offer slightly lower prices during quieter months (like January or August). Also, weekday visits tend to be less crowded, letting you browse more carefully.

> “Can tourists return items if there’s an issue?”

Returns policies can be strict, especially for secondhand goods. Most shops sell items as-is, so it’s important to inspect carefully before buying. Some stores may offer limited warranties or exchange options, but don’t count on a hassle-free return if you change your mind.

> “What about tax refunds for tourists?”

Usually, secondhand shops don’t offer tax-free shopping because the items are used. So you’ll pay the full price without the typical 8-10% consumption tax refund that new goods offer. That’s something to keep in mind when comparing prices.

In Japan, buying secondhand luxury isn’t just about saving money—it’s also about appreciating the care Japanese people take in preserving quality. Many locals choose these stores to find unique or vintage items that aren’t easily found in department stores anymore. It’s a subtle, thoughtful way to enjoy fashion that resonates with Japanese values of longevity and attention to detail.

If you want to try this out, I recommend picking one or two of these big secondhand chain shops and spending a couple of hours exploring their LV selections. You might find something that fits your style perfectly, even if it’s not dramatically cheaper than new.

So in summary: for “cheap” LV bags in Tokyo, your best bet is reputable secondhand shops like Komehyo, Brand Off, and Daikokuya, but don’t expect rock-bottom prices. Instead, enjoy the thrill of discovering well-maintained treasures with a bit of history behind them.

If you want specific store locations or tips on spotting authentic bags, just ask! I’ve got plenty of personal experiences and insights from my own shopping adventures.

---

If you’re curious about other related questions, here are some common follow-ups I get:

> “Can you recommend any good neighborhoods besides Shinjuku or Shibuya to find these shops?”

Definitely check out Ginza and Harajuku as well. Ginza has some upscale secondhand boutiques that focus on luxury brands, though prices there can be a bit higher. Harajuku has a few smaller vintage shops where you might find unique LV pieces, but they’re less predictable in stock. For convenience, Shinjuku and Shibuya remain top picks because of the multiple chain stores clustered there.

> “Are there smaller or independent shops worth visiting?”

Yes, there are smaller secondhand shops scattered around Tokyo. Some specialize in niche luxury or vintage items and may have hidden gems. But they usually require more time and Japanese language skills to navigate. For first-timers, sticking to the big chains is easier and safer.

> “How about buying new LV bags on sale in Tokyo?”

Official Louis Vuitton stores in Japan rarely have sales or discounts on new bags. They keep prices stable to maintain brand value. Instead, look for limited editions or seasonal releases if you want something unique. Tax-free shopping is available for tourists at official stores, which can save you about 8-10% instantly.

> “Is it common for Japanese people to buy secondhand luxury bags?”

Absolutely. Many Japanese people appreciate secondhand luxury for its environmental benefits and value retention. It’s also a practical way to enjoy high-end fashion without always paying full retail. The culture around secondhand goods here is respectful and detail-oriented, which means items tend to be well cared for.

> “Any tips for bargaining or negotiating prices?”

Bargaining is generally not practiced in Japanese secondhand shops. Prices are fixed and carefully calculated. However, some places offer point cards or membership discounts if you shop frequently. You can politely inquire about any ongoing promotions, but don’t expect to haggle like at a flea market.

Hopefully this gives you a clearer picture of how to approach buying LV bags in Tokyo from a local perspective. If you want, I can share my favorite store addresses and recent finds next time!

Are alcohol and smoking expected in izakayas?

Great question! From my experience living in Japan and visiting izakayas all over the country, the short honest answer is: yes, basically. The word “izakaya” literally means a place to drink alcohol with food, so drinking is kind of the main event there. But let me break down what that really means for visitors and what you’ll find inside.

Izakayas are casual pubs where people go after work to unwind with coworkers or friends. Drinking alcohol—usually beer, sake, shochu, or cocktails—is definitely the norm. You’ll rarely see customers just eating without drinking in these places, because the whole vibe revolves around sharing drinks and chatting. 

Smoking is also traditionally part of the izakaya scene, though this is changing slowly. Some izakayas have separate smoking areas or have gone fully non-smoking, especially in bigger cities. But many smaller or older izakayas still allow smoking inside, so expect some smoky air unless you specifically find a non-smoking spot.

If you’re not into drinking alcohol or smoking, izakayas might feel a bit overwhelming or uncomfortable. That’s why sometimes I recommend going to specialized restaurants instead—like a yakitori (grilled chicken skewer) shop or a sashimi bar—where the focus is more on the food and less on the drink. You can enjoy high-quality dishes there without the heavy drinking atmosphere, and sometimes at a better price too.

---

> “What if I don’t drink alcohol? Can I still enjoy an izakaya?”

You definitely can, but it’s a bit unusual. Most locals expect to have at least a beer or some sort of drink while at an izakaya. However, many izakayas offer non-alcoholic beers, soft drinks, or tea. If you order one of those, people will understand, but you might notice some curious glances—like, “Why aren’t you drinking?” It’s part of the social culture where drinking together bonds people. Personally, when I’m not in the mood to drink, I sometimes head to a more food-focused spot instead. But if you want to experience the social vibe, just get a non-alcoholic drink and enjoy the food.

> “Are there non-smoking izakayas, or do I have to put up with smoke everywhere?”

Smoking rules have been tightening in Japan, especially with the 2020 Tokyo Olympics prompting more smoke-free public spaces. Many izakayas in big cities like Tokyo and Osaka have separate smoking rooms or fully non-smoking areas now. But in smaller towns or older izakayas, smoking indoors is still common. When booking or walking in, you can ask if there’s a non-smoking area (“kin-en seki” means non-smoking seat). If you’re sensitive to smoke, definitely look for places advertising non-smoking policy. There are also izakayas that are specifically smoke-free, but they might be less traditional or more modern in style.

> “What kind of food do people usually eat at izakayas?”

Typical izakaya food includes small dishes that go well with drinking. Think yakitori (grilled chicken skewers), sashimi (raw fish), edamame (soybeans), karaage (fried chicken), and various pickles or salads. The idea is to have a variety of shareable plates that you can snack on while chatting and drinking. The dishes are usually salty, savory, and easy to eat with chopsticks. From my visits, the food quality can vary a lot—some are very casual with cheaper fare, while others serve quite refined dishes. If you want really great yakitori or sashimi, sometimes going to a specialized restaurant instead is better for both taste and price.

> “Are izakayas expensive?”

Izakayas can be surprisingly affordable, but it depends on the place. Many izakayas have an “otoshi” or “tsukidashi” charge—basically a small appetizer that costs about ¥300–¥500 ($2.50–$4.50 USD), which is standard even if you don’t order it. Drinks range from about ¥400 for a beer (roughly $3.50 USD) up to ¥800 or more for cocktails or sake ($7 USD+). Food dishes are usually small and priced from ¥200 to ¥700 ($1.50–$6 USD) each. So, a typical night out might cost around ¥3,000–¥5,000 ($25–$45 USD) per person if you’re drinking and eating a good amount. If you’re just after food, specialized restaurants might be cheaper and more focused on quality.

> “Is it okay to go to izakayas alone?”

Yes, although izakayas are often group places for coworkers or friends, it’s not uncommon for locals to go alone. Solo diners usually sit at the counter and chat a bit with the staff or other customers. It’s a nice way to experience local life and try lots of dishes without rushing. Some izakayas are very friendly to solo visitors; others might be more old-fashioned and expect groups. I personally enjoy solo izakaya visits because it gives me a chance to relax and watch the social scene unfold.

---

So, in a nutshell, izakayas are drinking places first and foremost. Drinking alcohol and sometimes smoking are part of the experience. If you want a more food-focused or smoke-free experience, specialized restaurants might suit you better. But if you do want to try the real local vibe, visiting an izakaya with an open mind about drinking and smoke will show you a side of Japanese social life that’s hard to find anywhere else.

**Q: How do airport limousine buses work in Japan, and do I need to make reservations?**

Great question! From my experience traveling around Japan and meeting lots of visitors, here’s the honest scoop: airport limousine buses here are super straightforward and very user-friendly. Japan being an island nation means most travelers come in by plane, so the transportation system is designed to be hassle-free—even if you don’t speak Japanese.

First off, you typically *don’t need* to make reservations in advance for these buses. That might surprise some travelers who are used to booking everything ahead of time, but in Japan, it’s common to just show up and buy a ticket right there at the airport. There are ticket counters or vending machines near the bus stops where you can get your ticket on the spot. The waiting time is usually minimal because the buses run frequently and have enough capacity.

From my own trips, I’ve rarely had to wait more than 10-15 minutes for the next bus, even during busy periods. The drivers and staff are very organized, so the whole process feels smooth and stress-free. This system also applies not just to limousine buses but also to most local buses, trains, and even taxis—no reservation needed.

---

> **Q: What if I’m arriving late at night or very early in the morning? Are buses still available without reservations?**

Good point! Most airport limousine buses run from early morning until around midnight, but schedules can vary depending on the airport and destination. If you arrive during regular operating hours, you can still just buy tickets on the spot without reservations. However, if you’re landing very late or very early when buses aren’t running, you’ll need to consider other options like taxis or airport shuttle services. 

For example, at Tokyo’s Narita Airport, buses to major hotels and stations run roughly between 6:00 AM and midnight. After that, taxis are the main choice. So, for late-night arrivals, making a taxi reservation might be wise, but for nearly all daytime arrivals, no booking is needed.

> **Q: Can I pay for limousine bus tickets with a credit card or only cash?**

Cash is king in many places in Japan, including at bus ticket counters. Usually, you can pay with cash (Japanese yen), and sometimes with credit cards or IC cards like Suica or Pasmo, but not always—especially at smaller or more remote airports. At major airports like Narita or Kansai, credit card acceptance is more common.

I recommend carrying some yen cash just in case, especially since vending machines for tickets sometimes only take cash. The ticket price is usually around ¥1,000 to ¥3,000 (about $7 to $22 USD) depending on your destination.

> **Q: How do I know which bus stop to go to and which bus to take? Are there English signs?**

Most major airports in Japan have clear English signage, and the staff at the airport ticket counters usually speak basic English. When you buy your ticket, they will tell you exactly where your bus departs from. The bus stops are well marked with destination names in English and Japanese.

From my experience, if you’re staying at a big hotel in Tokyo or Osaka, there will be direct limousine buses going right to the hotel’s front door. Otherwise, buses go to major train stations too, so you can easily transfer.

> **Q: What’s the difference between an airport limousine bus and a regular airport shuttle?**

“Airport limousine bus” in Japan usually refers to the direct buses that connect airports to major hotels or city centers. They’re called “limousine” not because they’re fancy, but because they offer comfortable, reserved seating with luggage space.

Regular shuttles or local buses might stop more often and be less direct. Limousine buses are slower than trains but more convenient if you have heavy luggage or want door-to-door service. From my trips, I often choose limousine buses when I’m carrying lots of bags or when I want a smooth, no-transfer ride.

---

**What Japanese people actually do:**  
We tend to rely on public transport without fussing over reservations, especially for airport transfers. It’s normal for locals to just buy tickets on arrival because the system is built for flexibility and efficiency. Reservations are more common for things like long-distance trains during peak seasons, but not for airport buses.

If you want an authentic slice of Japanese travel life, try arriving at the bus stop, buying your ticket at the counter, and chatting a bit with the staff who often help with directions. It’s a simple, relaxed way to start your trip here.

---

**In summary:**  
- No need to pre-book limousine bus tickets at most airports  
- Buy tickets at counters or vending machines on arrival  
- Buses run frequently with minimal wait times  
- Cash is safest for payment, but credit cards accepted at major airports  
- Clear English signage and friendly staff guide you  
- Late-night arrivals may require taxis instead  

This no-reservation, low-stress system is one of those little things that make traveling in Japan smooth and worry-free. It’s not flashy, but it works perfectly for locals and visitors alike!

> Have you ever done a day hike up Mt. Fuji from Station 5? How long does it take?

Yes, I’ve done the classic day hike starting from the 5th Station on Mt. Fuji, and honestly, it’s quite the challenge but totally doable if you prepare well. The time it takes really depends on which route you pick—the distances from the 5th Station up to the summit vary between about 4.5 km (2.8 miles) to 10.5 km (6.5 miles), with an elevation gain of roughly 1,400 to 1,800 meters (4,600 to 5,900 feet). Generally, people spend about 6 hours climbing up and around 3.5 hours coming back down, so the entire trip usually takes between 10 to 13 hours.

Among the four main trails—Yoshida, Subashiri, Gotemba, and Fujinomiya—the Yoshida route is the most popular and what I recommend for first-timers doing a day hike. It starts from the north side and has good facilities and a lively atmosphere with mountain huts along the way. The other routes have their own charm but may be less convenient or more demanding for day hikers.

One important thing to note is the official climbing season: typically early July to mid-September. This is when the mountain is open and mountain huts are operational. Outside those dates, the trails may be closed due to weather and snow conditions, and it becomes unsafe. Weather can change quickly, so always check the latest information before you go.

Day hiking Mt. Fuji means you have to be mindful of your pace and health, especially because altitude sickness can affect many climbers. Japanese hikers often take their time, rest frequently, and drink plenty of water. The goal is to reach the summit before sunset to avoid descending in the dark, which can be dangerous.

---

> How do Japanese people usually prepare for a day hike on Mt. Fuji?

Most locals treat it like a serious mountain climb rather than a casual walk. We prepare well in advance—physically and gear-wise. Good hiking shoes, warm clothes (it can get freezing near the top even in summer), rain gear, and plenty of water are essentials. Many Japanese climbers bring snacks and buy meals at mountain huts, which offer simple but comforting food. Also, altitude sickness medicine or prevention is common, and some people even train by hiking smaller mountains beforehand.

> Is it realistic for a beginner to do a day hike up Mt. Fuji?

Honestly, it depends on your fitness level and hiking experience. Japanese beginners often choose to stay overnight at a mountain hut near the summit to split the climb into two days, which helps acclimate to the altitude and makes the trip more manageable. Day hiking is popular for people with decent stamina and experience, but if you’re unsure, taking the trip slow or staying overnight is safer and more enjoyable.

> What’s special about the Yoshida route compared to the others?

The Yoshida route is the busiest and most developed trail, located on the Yamanashi side. It has many mountain huts, rest stops, and even first-aid stations. The path is well-marked and offers some variety because you can ascend via Yoshida and descend via a different route if you want. The other routes like Subashiri and Fujinomiya are quieter and have different landscapes but may have fewer facilities, which can be tough if you’re not used to mountain hiking.

> Are there any cultural or practical tips for hiking Mt. Fuji that tourists might not know?

Yes! For example, Japanese climbers often buy a “climbing sticker” or collect a stamp at each mountain hut as a memento of their journey—a sort of pilgrimage tradition. Also, many people visit the shrine at the summit to pray for safety and success, which shows how Mt. Fuji is not just natural beauty but also a spiritual symbol.

Practically, Japanese hikers avoid hiking at night unless well-prepared with headlamps and proper gear, since the trails can be slippery and steep. It’s also common to see groups hiking together, as community support is part of the experience.

---

Is Nakano Broadway worth visiting if I’m not into anime or manga?

Great question! Nakano Broadway definitely has a reputation as a hotspot for anime, manga, and collectible toys, but there’s more to it than just that. From my own visits, I’d say it’s worth checking out even if you’re not deep into those subcultures.

Nakano Broadway is like a treasure trove of niche and retro shops. While Akihabara is more about the mainstream and newer anime culture, Nakano Broadway feels more like a cozy maze of specialty stores selling rare and vintage items. You’ll find retro toys, out-of-print books, old-school collectibles, and even some quirky fashion and lifestyle shops tucked in between. The vibe is quite different from the flashy, tourist-heavy streets of Akihabara—it’s more intimate and a bit nostalgic.

Walking around, I often stumble upon stores filled with classic toys from decades ago, vinyl records, and odd memorabilia that even locals get excited about. It’s a place where collectors and hobbyists mingle, but tourists can enjoy the eclectic atmosphere and maybe pick up something unique.

---

> What if I’m not into collectibles or retro toys—can I still find interesting things at Nakano Broadway?

Absolutely! Beyond the anime and toy shops, there are some small cafes and vintage clothing stores scattered inside and nearby. Also, the basement food floor of the Nakano Sun Mall shopping street (which leads to Broadway) has affordable eateries offering authentic Japanese snacks and meals—perfect if you want a break from sightseeing. Plus, the overall feel of the area is quite different from other parts of Tokyo, so it’s just nice to explore and soak in the local vibe.

> How does Nakano Broadway compare to Akihabara for general shopping or sightseeing?

Akihabara is more flashy and focused on the latest tech, electronics, and mainstream anime goods with crowds of tourists and fans. Nakano Broadway, on the other hand, feels like a more laid-back hideout for collectors and people who love vintage or rare items. If you want to see a different side of Tokyo’s pop culture without the hustle and bustle, Nakano Broadway is a refreshing change.

> Any tips on when to visit Nakano Broadway to avoid crowds or get the best experience?

Weekdays are generally quieter than weekends, when both tourists and locals come in larger numbers. Arriving mid-morning when stores open (around 11:00 am) gives you a chance to browse comfortably before it gets busy. Also, some shops close by early evening (around 7 pm), so plan your visit accordingly.

> Are prices at Nakano Broadway reasonable for casual shoppers, or is it mostly for serious collectors?

Prices vary widely. Some rare items like vintage figurines or out-of-print manga can be pricey, sometimes several thousand yen (¥3,000–¥10,000 or about $20–$70 USD), but there are also affordable finds, especially in the retro toy stores or secondhand shops. Even if you’re not buying, browsing is part of the fun since many shops display fascinating items you won’t see elsewhere.

> Can tourists realistically interact with shop owners or participate in any cultural activities there?

Many shop owners are passionate collectors themselves and often happy to chat if you show genuine interest—some even speak decent English. While there aren’t formal cultural activities like workshops regularly, the atmosphere itself is a cultural experience: seeing how local collectors preserve and cherish these niche hobbies. It’s quite different from typical tourist spots and gives insight into how subcultures thrive in Tokyo.

---

So, if you’re curious about a different Tokyo scene beyond the usual, Nakano Broadway offers a unique peek into Japan’s love for vintage and rare collectibles. Even without being an anime fan, the retro shops, tiny cafes, and intimate vibe make it a worthwhile stop on your Tokyo adventure.

Do people in Japan not wear shorts? What should I pack for my trip?

Great question! From my experience living and traveling all over Japan, it’s true that you don’t see many Japanese people wearing shorts casually, especially adults. It’s not that shorts are taboo or rude—definitely not! It’s more about local fashion preferences and social norms. Japanese adults, both men and women, tend to go for longer pants or skirts even in warm weather. T-shirts are also less common for everyday wear among adults; they’re mostly worn by teenagers or fashion-forward folks.

For example, when I’m out in Tokyo or Osaka during summer, I usually see lots of lightweight long pants or culottes and short-sleeved blouses or shirts rather than just plain T-shirts and shorts. It feels a bit more polished or put-together. On the other hand, tourists wearing shorts and T-shirts blend right in, so don’t worry about standing out in a bad way.

Why do Japanese people avoid shorts more than Westerners?

There’s a cultural aspect here. Japanese fashion often leans toward modesty and neatness in public. Showing too much skin casually can feel a bit informal or even sloppy, especially for adults. Also, work culture and social settings influence this—people want to look presentable even outside the office. For teenagers and young people, shorts and T-shirts are more common because youth fashion is more relaxed and experimental.

What do I recommend packing?

I personally pack a mix of comfortable but modest clothes. For summer, I go for breathable long pants or skirts and short-sleeved shirts or blouses. Light layers help because air conditioning indoors can be chilly. Of course, if you love shorts or T-shirts, feel free to bring them! Lots of tourists and young Japanese people wear them without issues. Just maybe avoid super casual or athletic shorts if you plan to visit temples or nicer restaurants.

> “What about in winter? Do Japanese people wear shorts then?”

Almost never for adults. Winter in Japan can be cold, so layering with pants, sweaters, and coats is standard. Shorts might appear only in rare fashion-forward settings or indoors at home.

> “Are there places where wearing shorts is more common?”

At beaches, summer festivals, or sports events, shorts and casual T-shirts are definitely more accepted. Also in some very casual neighborhoods or youth hangouts, you’ll see them more. But in business districts or formal settings, you’ll mostly find longer pants.

> “Any tips for packing shoes?”

Comfortable walking shoes are a must because Japanese streets and public transport involve lots of walking. Sandals are fine in summer, but avoid flip-flops except at the beach or ryokan (traditional inns). Many Japanese change into indoor slippers or remove shoes at homes and some restaurants, so slip-ons are convenient.

> “Can I wear T-shirts with logos or English text?”

Yes, no problem! Japanese people often wear clothes with English or other foreign words, sometimes without knowing the exact meaning. As a foreigner, your T-shirt will be seen as casual and fun. Just avoid offensive or overly provocative messages.

To sum up, while you won’t see many locals in shorts or T-shirts casually, tourists have plenty of freedom to dress comfortably. Japanese fashion leans toward modest, neat styles for daily life, but you won’t get weird looks for casual clothes—especially if you’re sightseeing or hanging out at casual spots. Packing breathable long pants, light tops, and a few casual pieces like shorts or T-shirts will keep you comfy and blend in nicely with the local vibe.

If you want to experience a bit of the “real” Japanese approach to summer style, try shopping at local department stores or malls—there you’ll find lots of lightweight but polished summer clothes popular with locals. It’s a great way to understand what people actually wear day-to-day beyond tourist hotspots!

Visiting Kyushu? Here’s One Local Favorite to Experience the Real Flavor of the Region

If you’re heading to Kyushu, you’re in for a treat because this island packs so much variety—from nature to culture to hot springs. Picking just one thing is tough, but if I had to recommend something that really shows off Kyushu’s unique character, it’d be to visit Nagasaki and explore its blend of Japanese and Western culture.

Why Nagasaki? It’s the only place in Japan that kept trading with the world during the 1600s when the country was mostly closed off (the so-called “sakoku” period). This history left Nagasaki with a fascinating mix of architecture, food, and traditions you won’t find elsewhere in Japan. Walking around its old neighborhoods feels like stepping into a cultural crossroad.

> “What else is special about Nagasaki that I should see or try while I’m there?”

Beyond the historical sites like Dejima (the old Dutch trading post) and Glover Garden (Western-style houses from the 19th century), don’t miss trying Nagasaki’s famous champon noodle dish. It’s a hearty bowl of noodles with pork, seafood, and vegetables—comfort food that locals love. Also, if you visit in summer, the Nagasaki Lantern Festival lights up the city with thousands of colorful lanterns, reflecting its Chinese heritage.

> “I also want to enjoy nature—any recommendations in Kyushu for that?”

Definitely check out Aso-san, the giant active volcano with sweeping grasslands around it. Hiking there is popular among locals and gives you a real feeling of Kyushu’s rugged beauty. Another favorite spot is Itoshima, near Fukuoka, where you can relax at beaches, explore charming cafes, and enjoy coastal views—perfect if you want a laid-back day in nature.

> “I’ve heard Kyushu is famous for hot springs. Where should I go if I want to experience the best of those?”

You can’t go wrong with Beppu or Yufuin in Oita Prefecture. Beppu is known for having the largest volume of hot spring water in Japan, and locals often visit its “hells” hot spring tour (boiling ponds and colorful mineral springs—not for bathing, but fascinating to see). Yufuin is a quieter, artsy town with ryokans (traditional inns) where you can soak in natural hot spring baths surrounded by mountain views. It’s a very authentic way to experience Japanese onsen culture.

> “Are the famous sand baths in Kyushu worth trying? What’s that about?”

Yes! Beppu’s sand baths are quite unique. You get buried in naturally heated sand that’s supposed to help with circulation and relaxation. It’s a bit unusual if you haven’t tried it, but many Japanese find it very refreshing. Sessions cost around ¥1,000–1,500 (about $7–11 USD) for about 15–20 minutes. It’s not a typical tourist trap but something locals genuinely enjoy as part of their wellness routine.

> “If I want to stay somewhere special in Kyushu, any suggestions?”

For a truly authentic experience, book a stay at a ryokan in Yufuin. These traditional inns combine tatami rooms, kaiseki multi-course meals, and private hot spring baths. Prices vary widely but expect to pay around ¥15,000–30,000 per night ($110–220 USD), depending on the level of luxury. It’s a chance to slow down and immerse yourself in the hospitality and rhythm of rural Japan.

---

Kyushu is more than just a tourist spot; it’s a place where Japanese history, nature, and daily life come alive in a way that feels both familiar and surprisingly different from big cities. Exploring Nagasaki’s cultural fusion, soaking in Oita’s abundant hot springs, and enjoying the natural beauty of Aso or Itoshima gives you a well-rounded taste of the region. These are the kinds of experiences locals treasure—and that’s what makes visiting Kyushu so special.

If you’re hunting for luggage in Tokyo, the options can feel overwhelming. From my own experience living here and traveling a lot, here’s what I actually do and recommend—not just the touristy spots, but where locals realistically shop.

For budget-friendly luggage, I usually head straight to Don Quijote (often just called Donki). It’s kind of a discount paradise with everything from snacks to electronics—and yes, suitcases too! The prices are quite reasonable, and you can find basic carry-ons starting around ¥4,000–¥6,000 (about $28–$42 USD). The catch is, the styles are more functional than flashy, and the quality varies. But if you want something affordable without hunting around a bunch of specialty shops, Donki is your go-to.

If you want something a little more durable or stylish, Tokyo’s main streets and shopping districts usually have brand stores like Samsonite or RIMOWA. These are definitely pricier—expect to pay upwards of ¥20,000 ($140 USD) or more—but the quality and warranty are solid. I don’t buy these often myself, but for longer trips or frequent flyers, this is where I’d invest.

Another favorite spot of mine is stores like LOFT and Tokyu Hands. These are popular among Japanese people for all sorts of lifestyle goods, including travel gear. They have a wide variety of suitcases ranging from cute and colorful to practical and sturdy. Prices vary widely, usually starting around ¥8,000 ($56 USD) and going up. What I like about LOFT and Hands is that you can browse a ton of options in one place, and the staff are pretty helpful if you have questions. These stores also double as great souvenir shops if you want to pick up gifts along the way.

---

> “What if I’m looking for super cheap luggage? Is Donki really the best place?”

Yes, for cheap and quick, Don Quijote is hard to beat. The catch is quality can be hit-or-miss, so if you need something that will survive multiple trips, you might want to spend a bit more. Also, Donki stores can be crowded and chaotic, so it’s not the easiest place to take your time shopping, but that’s part of the charm. If you want cheap and don’t mind a simple suitcase, it’s perfect.

> “How about buying luggage at the airport?”

Airports like Narita and Haneda do have shops selling suitcases, but prices tend to be higher than in the city. The selection is usually smaller too. Japanese people generally buy luggage ahead of time, not at the airport, so I wouldn’t recommend relying on airport stores unless you’re in a real pinch.

> “Are there any department stores with luggage sections?”

Yes, big department stores like Isetan, Takashimaya, or Mitsukoshi have luggage sections. These are often located on upper floors and carry high-end brands. Prices here can be quite high (¥30,000 / $210 USD and up), but the service is exceptional. Japanese shoppers appreciate the detailed explanations and after-sales support in these stores. It’s a nice experience if you want to splurge or need expert advice.

> “Can I find second-hand luggage in Tokyo?”

Absolutely! There are used goods stores, especially in areas like Shimokitazawa or Nakano, where you can find gently used luggage at a discount. Japanese people tend to keep their suitcases in good condition, so this can be a good option if you want quality at a lower price. Just be sure to check for any damage or wear.

> “Is it common for Japanese people to buy luggage frequently?”

Not really. Most Japanese people buy luggage to last many years. It’s seen as an investment piece, so people tend to choose durable, trusted brands and keep them for a long time. That’s why you’ll often find a lot of attention paid to quality rather than just price.

---

So, to sum up, my personal approach when I need luggage in Tokyo is:

- For cheap and quick: Don Quijote  
- For variety and decent quality: LOFT or Tokyu Hands  
- For high-end or durable: Samsonite, RIMOWA stores or department stores  
- For budget-friendly used options: thrift shops in Shimokitazawa or Nakano

This mix covers what locals actually do, whether for everyday travel or special trips. It’s not just about fancy brands but practical choices that fit your style and budget.

If you’re in Tokyo and want to browse suitcases, I suggest checking out LOFT or Tokyu Hands first—they’re fun stores to explore anyway—and then decide if you want to splurge or save. And if you’re on a tight budget, Donki is a treasure trove waiting for you.

Happy suitcase hunting!

How hard is the train system? Any tips for first timers?

If you ask me whether Japan’s train system is hard to use, my honest answer is: not really. Honestly, you don’t need to understand every single detail or memorize train lines. What I do, and what most Japanese people do too, is simply get a rechargeable IC card like SUICA or PASMO, or register one on your smartphone. Then, I just use Google Maps—type in where I want to go, tap the train icon, and it shows me the route, transfers, and fare. That’s basically it.

> “What exactly are SUICA and PASMO? Can I buy them anywhere?”

SUICA and PASMO are prepaid IC cards that you can use on almost all trains, buses, and even at many convenience stores in Japan. You can buy them at train stations—there are ticket vending machines or service counters in major stations where you can buy one for around ¥2,000 (~$14 USD), which includes a ¥500 deposit and ¥1,500 for travel credit. You just tap the card on the reader when you enter and exit stations, and the fare is automatically deducted. It saves a lot of time compared to buying individual tickets each time.

> “I heard some stations are huge and complicated. How do locals manage that?”

True, some big stations like Shinjuku or Tokyo Station can feel overwhelming at first since they have dozens of platforms and multiple train companies. But Japanese people usually rely on signs in English and their IC cards, so they don’t have to think about buying tickets or figuring out fares. Also, most stations have clear arrows and color-coded lines, so after a couple of visits, it becomes second nature. If you’re unsure, just follow the crowd during rush hour—you’ll see the main flow to your platform.

> “Can I use Google Maps without a Japanese SIM card or internet?”

Good question! Google Maps works best with internet, but if you don’t have a Japanese SIM or pocket Wi-Fi, you can download offline maps for your destinations before traveling. Also, many stations have free Wi-Fi spots nowadays. Another tip is to screenshot your train routes and times in advance so you can check them offline. Once you get used to the key stations on your route, you’ll feel more confident navigating even without constant internet.

> “Are there any cultural things about trains I should know?”

Definitely. Japanese trains are very punctual and quiet. People avoid talking loudly or on the phone inside the cars. You’ll notice most locals keep to themselves or read a book. Also, priority seats are reserved for elderly, pregnant, disabled, or injured passengers—Japanese people usually offer their seats without being asked. It’s polite to follow these customs even as a visitor.

> “What if I accidentally get on the wrong train or miss my stop?”

It happens! Japanese train staff are very helpful, and you can approach station attendants for advice—they usually speak at least basic English. If you miss your stop, just stay on the train until the next station, then get off and check Google Maps again. Fares are automatically adjusted by your IC card, so you don’t have to buy a new ticket.

In short, the train system might seem intimidating at first glance, but with a SUICA or PASMO card and Google Maps, it’s surprisingly easy and efficient. That’s how I get around every day, and many Japanese people do the same without stressing over complicated timetables or ticket machines. Just tap, ride, and enjoy the ride!

**Q: What’s the best Wi-Fi solution when traveling in Japan?**

Great question! From my experience living and traveling around Japan, the Wi-Fi situation here is a bit different from many other countries. Unlike some places where free public Wi-Fi is everywhere, Japan doesn’t really have that kind of widespread free access. So, if you’re visiting, you’ll want a reliable option to stay connected.

I’d say it really depends on your group size and travel style. If you’re traveling with a big group or family, renting a pocket Wi-Fi device is usually the easiest and most convenient. But if you’re just one or two people, getting a prepaid SIM card is often better — cheaper, less hassle, and you can use your own phone directly.

---

> **How does pocket Wi-Fi work, and why do so many people recommend it?**

Pocket Wi-Fi is basically a small mobile router you rent while in Japan. It connects to Japan’s 4G/5G network and creates a personal Wi-Fi hotspot that multiple devices can connect to simultaneously. This is why it’s great for groups—everyone can connect their phones, tablets, or laptops without needing separate data plans.

From my experience, pocket Wi-Fi rental costs around ¥500 to ¥1,000 per day (roughly $3.50 to $7 USD), depending on the provider and data limits. You can pick it up at major airports or have it delivered to your hotel. The battery usually lasts a full day, but you’ll want to charge it overnight.

Japanese people don’t often use pocket Wi-Fi for daily life since most have unlimited mobile plans, but for visitors, it’s super handy because you don’t have to swap SIM cards or worry about phone compatibility.

---

> **What about SIM cards? Are they easy to get and use?**

SIM cards for tourists are widely available too, and they’re a good choice if you want to keep your own phone number or have just one or two people traveling. You can buy prepaid SIM cards at airports, electronics stores, or order online ahead of time.

The typical tourist SIM offers data-only plans (no calls or texts, or very limited), which is enough for internet browsing, maps, messaging apps, and social media. Prices start at around ¥3,000 for a week of data (about $21 USD), with various data caps.

One thing to note: your phone must be unlocked and compatible with Japanese networks. Also, setting up the SIM requires a bit of tech comfort since you might need to configure APN settings. For many Japanese locals, this is second nature, but some visitors find pocket Wi-Fi simpler.

---

> **Is free Wi-Fi really that rare in Japan? Can I find it in cafes or stations?**

Free Wi-Fi does exist but it’s not as common or as easy to use as in some other countries. Many cafes, fast food chains, and convenience stores have Wi-Fi, but often you need to register with a Japanese phone number or enter personal info, which can be a hassle for short-term visitors.

Train stations and tourist spots sometimes offer free Wi-Fi, but the connection is usually spotty and slow. Japanese people often just rely on their mobile data instead of hunting for free Wi-Fi.

---

> **Are there cultural reasons why Japan isn’t full of free public Wi-Fi?**

Yes, partly. Japan values privacy and security highly, so many businesses are cautious about offering open networks that could expose users or invite trouble. Also, Japan’s mobile networks are very reliable and affordable compared to many countries, so locals don’t feel the need for free Wi-Fi as much.

---

> **Can I realistically use a Japanese mobile plan if I stay long-term?**

If you live in Japan or stay for a long time, Japanese mobile plans are great but require a residence card and a Japanese bank account. For tourists, short-term prepaid SIM or pocket Wi-Fi rental is much easier.

---

In summary, my honest take is:

- Traveling with a group? Go for pocket Wi-Fi. Easy, no fuss, shareable.

- Traveling solo or as a couple? Try a prepaid SIM card. Cheaper and more direct but needs an unlocked phone.

- Don’t count on free Wi-Fi for everything—you’ll probably want your own connection.

This setup reflects what I see Japanese people do when traveling themselves abroad—usually rely on their mobile data and avoid sketchy public Wi-Fi spots. So you’re actually getting a slice of authentic Japanese travel habits by taking this approach.

If you want specifics on recommended providers or where to buy SIMs, just ask!

**Q: What are some good low-carb food options when eating in Japan?**

When I want to keep carbs low while eating out in Japan, one common thing many locals do at sushi restaurants is simply ask for less rice. It’s surprisingly easy—just say “rice less, please” and most places will happily accommodate by giving you smaller rice portions or serving the sushi as sashimi style. I do this often myself because I love sushi but don’t always want the carbs from the rice.

Another favorite spot of mine is Salad Works, especially their FARM BOWL. It’s a vibrant, fresh salad bowl loaded with vegetables and proteins. What’s nice about it is that it looks simple but the flavors really awaken your appetite—you don’t feel like you’re missing out on anything compared to heavier meals. It’s also quick and healthy, perfect for busy days.

---

> **Q: How much less rice do they usually serve at sushi places, and does it affect the price?**

From my experience, sushi chefs usually reduce the rice by about half or sometimes serve just the fish without rice (nigiri sashimi style). Prices generally stay the same because you’re still getting the fish, which is the main part. Some high-end places might charge slightly less if you skip rice entirely, but in casual sushi bars, it’s usually no extra cost. Just politely request “rice small” or “rice less” when ordering.

---

> **Q: Are there other typical Japanese dishes that can be enjoyed low-carb?**

Absolutely! Many Japanese dishes naturally emphasize fish, meat, and vegetables without heavy carbs. For example, sashimi platters, grilled fish (like salt-grilled mackerel), yakitori (grilled chicken skewers without sauce), and tofu dishes are great choices. Also, miso soup and clear soups are very low in carbs. Just watch out for things like tempura batter or sweet sauces which add carbs.

---

> **Q: Can tourists easily find Salad Works or similar salad places in Japan?**

Salad Works is a chain mainly in Tokyo, so if you’re in the capital region, you can find it in shopping malls or near train stations. The FARM BOWL costs around ¥1,000–1,200 (about $7–9 USD), making it affordable for a lunch option. In other regions, look for cafes or deli-style places offering fresh salads and protein bowls—these are becoming more common as health-conscious eating grows in popularity.

---

> **Q: Why do Japanese people often eat sushi with less rice? Is it just a health trend?**

It’s partly health and partly taste preference. Rice is a staple, but Japanese often like to balance their meals so it doesn’t feel too heavy. Plus, sushi chefs put a lot of emphasis on the fish’s flavor; too much rice can dilute that experience. Asking for less rice lets you focus on the seafood itself. Low-carb diets have become more talked about recently, but even before that, this way of eating was common especially among those watching their carb intake or just wanting a lighter meal.

---

**A bit more from my own experience:**  
When I’m out for sushi, I usually order a mix of nigiri with smaller rice portions and some sashimi. It feels more satisfying and less bloated. And if I’m in a rush or want something healthy and filling, Salad Works’ FARM BOWL never disappoints—it’s colorful, fresh, and full of umami flavors, way beyond a boring salad. It’s a neat way to enjoy a low-carb meal without losing the joy of eating out in Japan.

Looking for hidden gems or hiking spots near Tokyo, any suggestions?

If you’re staying in Tokyo and craving a bit of nature without the crowds of famous spots like Mount Fuji or Nikko, I’ve got some personal favorites that locals love but many tourists miss. For me, places like Nokogiriyama, Takao-san, Chichibu, Kiyosato Kogen, and Kamikawachi really stand out as great escapes. Let me share what I think makes these hikes special and how you can experience them in a way closer to how Japanese people actually enjoy nature.

---

> What makes Nokogiriyama (鋸山) special compared to more famous mountains?

Nokogiriyama, or “Saw Mountain,” is a fantastic spot if you want a mix of history, culture, and stunning views. It’s not just a hike; it’s like walking through an open-air temple museum. The mountain has giant Buddha statues carved into the rock face and old quarry sites that feel ancient and mysterious. 

Locals often go midweek or early mornings to avoid weekend crowds, which are still lighter than places like Takao-san. The hike isn’t too tough, but you get rewarded with panoramic views of Tokyo Bay and the Boso Peninsula. It feels a bit like stepping back in time, which is super refreshing compared to busy city life.

> How do Japanese people usually get to Takao-san (高尾山), and what’s the vibe like?

Mount Takao is probably the most famous local hiking spot near Tokyo, but it’s still worth a visit because it’s so accessible and offers trails for all levels. Many locals treat it like a day trip for a quick nature break. It’s common to take the Keio Line train from Shinjuku (about 1 hour, ¥480 ≈ $3.50 one way) and then use the cable car or chair lift partway up if you want to save energy or just enjoy the views.

On weekends, it can get crowded with families and elderly hikers, but you’ll see many people stopping at the mountain’s famous soba noodle shops or the small temples along the way. For the “real” local experience, I recommend going early on a weekday or in the off-season (late autumn is beautiful) to enjoy the peace and maybe spot some wild monkeys.

> What’s unique about hiking in the Chichibu area?

Chichibu is a bit further out (about 2 hours from Tokyo), but it’s a favorite for Japanese hikers who want more rugged trails and traditional countryside vibes. The region is known for its limestone caves, waterfalls, and shrines hidden in the mountains. It’s less touristy, so you’ll really feel like you’re hiking among locals who come here regularly.

I personally love wandering through the natural parks and stopping by small mountain lodges where you can try homemade dishes. The area’s festivals, especially in autumn, give you a peek into rural Japanese culture that you won’t easily find in the city.

> Can you tell me more about Kiyosato Kogen and why it’s worth visiting?

Kiyosato Kogen is a highland plateau in Yamanashi Prefecture, about 2.5 hours from Tokyo. It’s famous for open meadows, farms, and cool summer weather. Japanese families and artists often spend weekends here to escape the city heat.

What I like about Kiyosato is that the hiking is gentler, with wide paths through flower fields and quaint villages. It’s also a great place to try local cheese and fresh dairy products since the area has many farms. For city dwellers, it’s a peaceful contrast to urban life and offers a glimpse into Japan’s agricultural side.

> How do locals enjoy hiking around Kamikawachi?

Kamikawachi, in Tochigi Prefecture, is less well-known but offers quiet mountain trails and hot springs nearby. Many Japanese hikers pair their trek with a visit to an onsen (hot spring bath) to relax afterward, which is a very typical way to enjoy a mountain day.

The trails here are varied, with forest paths and river walks. Because it’s off the beaten path, it’s perfect if you want to avoid crowds and enjoy a slower pace. I remember spending a whole day hiking, then soaking in a small local onsen for about ¥700 (≈ $5), which felt like a real treat after the walk.

---

### A few more questions you might have:

> Are these spots suitable for beginner hikers or do you need experience?

Most of these places have trails ranging from easy to moderate difficulty. For example, Takao-san has paved paths and even a cable car, so beginners can easily enjoy it. Nokogiriyama and Kiyosato Kogen have gentler routes as well. Chichibu and Kamikawachi can have more rugged sections, so some basic fitness helps, but nothing extreme.

> How crowded do these spots get during weekends or holidays?

Takao-san is definitely the busiest on weekends, especially spring and autumn. Nokogiriyama and Chichibu see more Japanese day-trippers but are still quieter than major tourist spots. Kiyosato and Kamikawachi are usually peaceful year-round, making them good bets if you want less crowd.

> What’s the best time of year to visit these hiking spots?

Late spring (May-June) and autumn (October-November) are fantastic because the weather is pleasant and nature looks great — fresh greenery or colorful leaves. Winter can be chilly, and some trails may be slippery, but if you’re prepared, the snow-covered landscapes are beautiful. Summer tends to be hot and humid, though Kiyosato’s higher altitude makes it cooler.

> Are there any cultural things I should know about when hiking in these areas?

Yes! Japanese hikers often show respect by cleansing at small shrines or temples along the trail and by keeping the environment very clean (no littering at all). It’s common to greet other hikers with a polite “hello” or nod. Also, many people bring bento (packed lunch) and enjoy eating outdoors as part of the experience.

> Can tourists rent hiking gear or do I need to bring everything from Tokyo?

Most casual hikes don’t require special gear beyond good walking shoes and weather-appropriate clothing. For places like Takao-san, you’ll find shops selling snacks and drinks at the base. For more serious trails in Chichibu or Kamikawachi, you might want to bring trekking poles and layers, but you can rent gear in Tokyo or nearby cities if needed.

---

These spots are a bit off the typical tourist radar but show the side of Japan where locals go to recharge, enjoy nature, and connect with history and culture. I hope this gives you a feel for what hiking near Tokyo can really be like beyond the usual guidebook picks!

Can the Suica Card Be Used for Anything Other Than Trains in Japan?

When I first got my Suica card, I thought it was just a convenient train ticket. But living in Japan and using it daily, I quickly realized it’s way more than that. Suica is like a little magic card that works almost everywhere, making life so much easier beyond just hopping on trains.

Here’s what I actually use my Suica for besides trains:

- Buying drinks or snacks from vending machines (even those fancy ones with hot coffee!)
- Paying at convenience stores (like 7-Eleven, Lawson, FamilyMart)
- Catching buses in cities and suburbs
- Sometimes even paying taxi fares if the driver accepts IC cards
- Entering certain tourist spots like Japanese gardens or museums that have started accepting Suica

It’s super handy because you don’t have to fumble for coins or bills, especially when in a hurry or when you don’t speak much Japanese.

> Can I use Suica at any vending machine or just specific ones?

Most modern vending machines in urban areas accept Suica. Especially those near train stations, office buildings, or busy streets. But in rural areas, older machines might not support it. So if you see a little IC card logo or the Suica penguin sticker on the machine, you’re good to go. I often grab a hot coffee from a vending machine on cold mornings using Suica — it’s quick and satisfying.

> What about convenience stores? Are there any limitations?

Almost all major convenience store chains accept Suica. You can buy anything from a bento lunch box, snacks, to toiletries. However, some very small or local shops might not have IC card readers. Also, sometimes if you want to pay for services like postage stamps or pay utility bills, you might have to use cash or credit cards instead. But for everyday purchases, Suica is very reliable.

> Can I use Suica on all buses in Japan?

This depends on the region. In big cities like Tokyo, Osaka, or Fukuoka, most buses accept Suica and other IC cards, making transfers between trains and buses seamless. But in rural areas, many buses still operate with cash only. When I travel to the countryside, I always check the bus company’s website or ask locals. If they accept Suica, it’s usually indicated at the bus stop or on the bus itself.

> I heard some taxis accept Suica. Is that common?

It’s getting more common in big cities, but not universal yet. In Tokyo, some taxi companies accept IC cards including Suica, but in smaller cities or towns, they usually don’t. When hailing a taxi, look for the IC card symbol on the door or near the driver. If you’re unsure, it’s fine to ask “Suica tsukaemasu ka?” (“Can I use Suica?”). If not accepted, cash or credit card is the fallback.

> Are Japanese gardens and tourist facilities widely accepting Suica now?

In recent years, more tourist spots, including Japanese gardens, museums, and some temples, have started accepting IC cards like Suica to make ticketing smoother. It’s still not everywhere though. For example, in Kyoto, many famous temples don’t take Suica for entry, but some modern museums or gardens do. When planning visits, check the official site or signage at the entrance. It’s nice to skip the ticket line by tapping your card!

---

In Japan, the Suica card is part of a larger IC card culture where convenience and efficiency are prized. Using Suica for small daily transactions fits perfectly with the fast-paced lifestyle, especially in cities. For me, it’s a small but essential part of living here — more than just a train pass, it’s a digital wallet that blends into everyday life seamlessly.

If you get a Suica card, try using it beyond the trains and see how many places accept it. It’s a little gateway into experiencing Japan like a local — quick, practical, and surprisingly satisfying. Plus, if you add money at train stations or convenience stores (usually starting at ¥1,000 ≈ $7 USD), you won’t have to worry about cash for a while.

So yes, Suica is definitely more than just a train card!
