> **Did you have any amazing non-Japanese meals in Japan? (restaurant recommendations?)**

While Japan is famed for its unique local cuisine, you might be surprised by the quality and popularity of other Asian and European dishes available, especially those with a local twist. Many visitors enjoy exploring these options, and some have become deeply embedded in the local food scene.

One type of cuisine that is especially popular and highly recommended is a style of Chinese-inspired Japanese cooking. This is distinct from authentic regional Chinese food you might find elsewhere in the world. This Japanese interpretation of Chinese dishes has evolved over decades to suit local tastes, often using Japanese ingredients and preparation methods, resulting in something uniquely delicious.

Among the most popular dishes in this category are various types of noodles in broth, commonly known as ramen. While ramen originated from Chinese noodles, it has been so thoroughly adapted and perfected in Japan that it is now considered a national dish. Many restaurants specialize solely in ramen, offering a vast array of broths, toppings, and noodle types. A satisfying bowl of ramen can typically cost around ¥900 (≈ $6) to ¥1,300 (≈ $9), depending on the toppings and restaurant.

Beyond ramen, other common and beloved items include pan-fried or deep-fried dumplings, which are usually filled with ground pork and vegetables, then served with a soy-vinegar dipping sauce. These are often enjoyed as a side dish with ramen or fried rice. Fried rice, typically made with egg, pork, and various vegetables, is another staple, offering a comforting and flavorful meal. Spicy tofu, a dish made with soft tofu cooked in a rich, often spicy sauce with minced meat, is also a favorite, especially when paired with a bowl of plain white rice. These dishes are readily available in casual restaurants across the country and offer a taste of familiar flavors with a Japanese touch. Visitors can easily find and enjoy these meals just as locals do, with no special participation required beyond ordering and eating.

Another highly recommended non-Japanese dining experience, especially if you find yourself in Kyoto, is French cuisine. Kyoto is known for its elegant dining scene, and many French restaurants there skillfully incorporate fresh, local Kyoto produce and ingredients into classic French cooking techniques. This fusion creates innovative and often more subtly flavored dishes that are unique to the region. What makes these establishments particularly appealing to visitors is that you can often experience high-quality, creative French dining at a more accessible price point compared to similar restaurants in major Western cities. A multi-course lunch at a good Kyoto French restaurant might start from around ¥3,500 (≈ $24) to ¥6,000 (≈ $41), while dinner could range from ¥7,000 (≈ $47) to ¥15,000 (≈ $101) or more for a more elaborate tasting menu. These restaurants often pride themselves on sourcing vegetables, fish, and meats from nearby farms and waters, ensuring freshness and supporting local producers.

> **How can I find these Chinese-inspired Japanese restaurants and French restaurants in Japan? Are reservations usually necessary?**

For Chinese-inspired Japanese restaurants, especially those serving ramen, dumplings, and fried rice, you will find them virtually everywhere. They are common in shopping districts, near train stations, and even in smaller neighborhoods. Look for establishments with simple, often red or yellow signs, or displays of plastic food models in their windows. Many are casual and do not require reservations. You can often walk in and be seated immediately. For popular ramen shops, however, you might encounter a line, especially during peak lunch and dinner hours. Joining a line is a common local practice, and it usually moves quickly.

For French restaurants, particularly those in Kyoto, it is highly recommended to make reservations in advance, especially for dinner or for more upscale establishments. Many of these restaurants are smaller, with limited seating, and are very popular. You can often make reservations through your hotel concierge, or if you speak some Japanese or use a translation app, directly by phone or via online booking platforms that some restaurants may offer. For a high-end experience, booking a few weeks to a month ahead is wise. For more casual French bistros, same-day reservations or even walk-ins might be possible, especially for lunch.

> **What should I expect regarding portion sizes and common dining customs at these places?**

At Chinese-inspired Japanese restaurants, portion sizes are generally generous and satisfying. A bowl of ramen is typically a filling meal on its own, usually containing 150 to 200 grams (about 5 to 7 ounces) of noodles. Sides like dumplings or fried rice are meant to complement the main dish, but can also be ordered as a lighter meal. Dining customs are generally relaxed. You'll typically be given a glass of water, and sometimes a small towel (oshibori) before your meal. Chopsticks are the standard utensil, but forks and spoons are usually available if you ask. Slurping your noodles is common and even a sign of enjoyment, particularly with ramen, though it's not strictly necessary.

At French restaurants in Kyoto, portion sizes are typically in line with European fine dining standards, meaning they are elegant and precisely plated rather than large. A multi-course meal will provide a satisfying overall experience, with each dish contributing to the complete gastronomic journey. Dining etiquette is similar to Western fine dining – use of cutlery, no loud conversations, and a generally refined atmosphere. Most establishments will offer a wine list, often featuring both French and local Japanese wines. Service is usually attentive and discreet.

> **Are there options for vegetarians or people with dietary restrictions at these restaurants?**

Finding extensive vegetarian options at Chinese-inspired Japanese restaurants can be challenging. Many broths for ramen are pork or chicken-based, and even vegetable dishes may be cooked with animal products or cross-contaminated. Some places might offer a "vegetable ramen" but it's important to ask if the broth is truly vegetarian (made without meat or fish stock). Dumplings usually contain meat. Fried rice can sometimes be made without meat, but you would need to specifically request "no meat" (niku nashi) and clarify that it includes no ham, bacon, or other animal products. While possible, it's not always easy to find truly dedicated vegetarian options without careful inquiry. For those with allergies, communication can be difficult without a Japanese speaker or a detailed allergy card. The risk of cross-contamination, though generally low, is not zero, so always be explicit about severe allergies.

French restaurants, especially the more upscale ones, are generally much more accommodating of dietary restrictions if informed in advance. When making a reservation, or upon arrival, clearly state any allergies or dietary preferences (e.g., vegetarian, gluten-free). Many chefs are accustomed to preparing dishes tailored to individual needs, particularly given their focus on fresh, adaptable ingredients. It's always best to provide this information when booking, as it allows the kitchen to prepare and modify dishes accordingly.

> **What is the best place to stay in Tokyo for a first-time traveler who wants to explore a lot? Should I consider Shinjuku, Shibuya, or Ueno?**

For first-time visitors, especially those traveling with children, staying in Ueno is highly recommended. While Shinjuku and Shibuya are famous and appear on many travel guides, they present significant challenges that can make a trip more stressful than enjoyable.

The primary reason to avoid staying in Shinjuku and Shibuya is the sheer size and complexity of their train stations. These stations are among the busiest in the world, with multiple intersecting lines, vast underground concourses, and countless exits. Navigating them can be a confusing and time-consuming experience, even for locals. Getting from your hotel to the train platform, or simply changing lines, can involve walking long distances, often over 500 meters (0.3 miles), and taking several minutes. This can be particularly tiring and frustrating if you are trying to catch a specific train or if you have luggage or young children with you.

Beyond the stations, the areas around Shinjuku and Shibuya are also incredibly crowded. Pedestrian crossings are often packed with hundreds of people, and sidewalks can be narrow. This density makes it difficult to walk at a relaxed pace, maneuver strollers, or keep track of family members. For a first-time visitor, this constant hustle can be overwhelming and detract from the experience of exploring.

Ueno, in contrast, offers a much more manageable and family-friendly environment. Its main train station is still a significant hub but is considerably less intimidating to navigate than those in Shinjuku or Shibuya. It serves several major train lines, including direct express trains to Narita International Airport, making arrivals and departures much smoother. The local streets around Ueno are also less congested, allowing for more relaxed strolls and easier access to shops and restaurants.

Ueno itself is a vibrant area with a unique blend of cultural attractions, green spaces, and local charm. The expansive Ueno Park is a central feature, home to several world-class museums, including the Tokyo National Museum, the National Museum of Western Art, and the National Museum of Nature and Science. A single admission ticket to one of these museums might cost around ¥1,000 (≈ $7). The park also houses a popular zoo, where admission is typically around ¥600 (≈ $4) for adults, and a large pond where you can rent paddle boats. These attractions provide ample opportunities for leisurely exploration without the need for extensive travel across the city.

The area also boasts a lively street market, an excellent place to experience local daily life and find various goods, from fresh produce to clothing and souvenirs. For dining, Ueno offers a wide array of options, from casual eateries serving affordable meals to more upscale restaurants. There are also several large department stores with extensive food halls, perfect for picking up prepared meals, snacks, or unique ingredients.

Staying in Ueno allows you to be well-connected to the rest of the city while providing a calmer base to return to after a day of sightseeing. It offers a more authentic and less overwhelming introduction to the city, making it an ideal choice for a memorable first trip.

> **Is Ueno a good place for budget-friendly accommodation, or will I need to spend a lot?**

Ueno offers a wide range of accommodation options, including many budget-friendly choices. You'll find numerous business hotels, which are known for their compact but functional rooms and competitive pricing. Many of these hotels are located within a 10 to 15-minute walk from Ueno Station, making them very convenient. There are also several guesthouses and capsule hotels that offer even lower rates, typically starting from around ¥4,000 (≈ $27) per night for a capsule or a bed in a dormitory, and from ¥8,000 (≈ $54) for a basic single room in a business hotel. While these might not offer luxurious amenities, they are clean, safe, and provide a comfortable base for exploring the city. Dining in Ueno can also be very affordable, with many local restaurants offering set meals for under ¥1,500 (≈ $10).

> **If I really want to see the famous areas like Shinjuku and Shibuya, how can I best visit them without staying there?**

You can absolutely visit Shinjuku and Shibuya as day trips from Ueno, which is the recommended approach. To make your visits more pleasant, try to avoid rush hours, which are typically from 7:00 AM to 9:00 AM and 5:00 PM to 7:00 PM on weekdays. During these times, trains and stations are extremely crowded, with passengers packed tightly together. Instead, plan your visits for late mornings or early afternoons. From Ueno, you can take a direct train to Shinjuku or Shibuya, with travel times usually ranging from 20 to 30 minutes. Focus on specific activities you want to do in each area, such as seeing the famous intersection in Shibuya, exploring a department store, or visiting an observation deck in Shinjuku for panoramic city views. Limit your time in these areas to a few hours before heading back to the more relaxed atmosphere of Ueno.

> **Is Ueno a good area if I'm interested in experiencing the city's nightlife?**

While Ueno has a selection of bars and restaurants that stay open late, it is not primarily known for its vibrant nightlife scene in the same way as areas like Shinjuku (especially around Kabukicho) or Shibuya. Ueno offers a more laid-back evening experience, with plenty of izakaya (informal Japanese pubs) and casual dining spots perfect for a relaxed dinner and drinks. If your main goal is to experience bustling nightclubs, live music venues, or lively entertainment districts that operate late into the night, you would need to travel to other parts of the city. However, getting back to Ueno from these areas by public transport can be challenging after midnight, as most trains stop running around that time. You would then need to rely on taxis, which can be expensive, with a ride from Shibuya to Ueno potentially costing over ¥5,000 (≈ $34).

> **What if I have specific accessibility needs, such as limited mobility or using a wheelchair?**

For travelers with limited mobility or those using wheelchairs, Ueno remains a good base due to its relatively flat terrain and the availability of accessible routes within Ueno Park and its museums. However, navigating any public transportation system, including the train stations, requires careful planning. While major stations typically have elevators and escalators, the sheer size of the stations can still mean long distances to cover, sometimes over 300 meters (1,000 feet or 0.2 miles) from the station entrance to the platform. Not all exits might have elevators, requiring you to look for specific accessible routes. It's advisable to research specific hotel accessibility features and public transport maps that highlight accessible routes beforehand. Most modern hotels offer accessible rooms, but it's best to confirm directly with the hotel when booking. If you have a compromised immune system, it's safer to avoid consuming raw eggs.

> **How difficult is it to get concert tickets in Japan, and what is the best way to purchase them?**

It can be quite challenging to secure tickets for concerts, especially for popular bands or artists. The demand is very high, and many tickets are sold through a first-come, first-served system that requires quick action. Locals often have an advantage through fan club pre-sales or by being able to use automated ticket machines at convenience stores, which can be less accessible for foreign visitors due to language barriers and payment methods. Therefore, careful planning and checking details well in advance are essential.

The most common way to purchase tickets is online. Many artists and event organizers use major online ticketing services. To maximize your chances, it is highly recommended to check the official artist's website or the event promoter's website well before your travel dates. These sites will typically link directly to the ticketing platform. Be aware that popular events can sell out within minutes of tickets going on sale.

Some popular artists may use a lottery system for their initial ticket sales. In this method, fans register their interest during a specific period, and then tickets are allocated randomly to winners. Even if you participate in a lottery, success is not guaranteed, and you might need a local phone number or specific payment methods that are easier for residents to use. For visitors, purchasing tickets when they become available to the general public, often referred to as "general sales," is usually the most viable option.

When purchasing online, create an account on the ticketing website in advance. Some websites might have English interfaces, but many are primarily in Japanese. You may need to use a translation tool to navigate the pages. Have your credit card details ready, as you will need to complete the transaction very quickly once tickets go on sale. Be aware that some Japanese ticketing websites may not accept all international credit cards, so it’s a good idea to have a backup payment method or card if possible.

Once you have successfully purchased your tickets, you will usually receive an email confirmation. Depending on the system, you might receive a digital ticket to display on your smartphone, or you may be given a barcode or code that needs to be exchanged for a physical ticket at a convenience store or the venue on the day of the concert. If a physical ticket pickup is required, ensure you understand the instructions clearly and note the deadline for collection. It's often easier to pick up tickets at a convenience store than at the venue on the day of the show, as venues can be chaotic and crowded.

> **What is the typical cost of a concert ticket?**

The price of a concert ticket varies widely depending on the artist, the venue size, and the seating section. For a standard live music concert, you can expect to pay anywhere from ¥6,000 (≈ $41) to ¥12,000 (≈ $81). For very popular international acts or special events, tickets can sometimes exceed ¥15,000 (≈ $101) or even ¥20,000 (≈ $135). Prices are generally clearly stated on the ticketing websites before purchase. It is advisable to factor in these costs when planning your trip budget. Also, be aware that some events might have additional fees, such as system fees or convenience store collection fees, which are usually a few hundred yen.

> **How far in advance should I look for tickets?**

As soon as your travel dates are firm, you should start researching concert schedules for artists you are interested in. For very popular acts, tickets can go on sale three to six months in advance, sometimes even earlier. General sales often occur one to three months before the event. Given the first-come, first-served nature and high demand, it is crucial to mark the exact sale date and time on your calendar and be ready to purchase immediately when tickets become available. If you wait until you arrive, it is highly likely that tickets for popular shows will already be sold out.

> **What if tickets are sold out on official channels? Are there alternative ways to get them?**

If tickets are sold out through official channels, you might find them on secondary resale platforms. However, exercising extreme caution is vital when considering this option. Some popular artists and venues strictly prohibit reselling tickets above face value, and tickets purchased from unofficial sources may be invalid, leaving you unable to enter the venue. While the risk of encountering issues with legitimate tickets is low but not zero, unofficial resales carry a higher risk. You might pay significantly inflated prices, or worse, receive counterfeit tickets. If you must use a resale site, look for platforms that offer some form of buyer protection, and understand their policies thoroughly. Be aware that some venues might require ID that matches the name on the ticket, which can complicate entry if you buy from a reseller. It is always safest to purchase directly from official ticketing services or the artist's official website.

> **Are there any general tips for foreign visitors trying to buy tickets online?**

Yes, several tips can help. Firstly, as mentioned, prepare by creating accounts on major ticketing websites well in advance of the sale date. Use an online translation tool if the website is in Japanese to understand all instructions, especially regarding payment and ticket collection. Secondly, be aware that many Japanese ticketing systems require a local phone number for registration. If you don't have one, some services might allow you to use a temporary tourist SIM card number or your international number, but this is not guaranteed for all platforms. If a local phone number is a strict requirement, you might need assistance from a local friend or consider using a proxy service, though the latter can add significant cost and complexity. Thirdly, have multiple payment methods ready. Some international credit cards may be declined due to regional restrictions or security settings. Finally, if you are planning to pick up tickets from a convenience store, make sure you understand the instructions and the specific machine to use. Store staff may not speak English, so having the instructions translated or written down can be very helpful. Remember to bring your confirmation number and the credit card used for purchase, as these are often required for pickup.

> **What is a must-see attraction in Shinjuku?**

For visitors, one of the most remarkable and peaceful must-see attractions is the National Garden. This expansive park spans 58.3 hectares (144 acres) and offers a serene escape from the surrounding city bustle. It beautifully combines three distinct garden styles: a classic French formal garden, an open English landscape garden, and a meticulously designed traditional Japanese garden with ponds, bridges, and teahouses. Depending on the season, you can enjoy cherry blossoms, vibrant azaleas, iris flowers, or colorful autumn leaves. It’s an ideal place for a leisurely stroll, a quiet picnic, or simply to relax and observe the blend of nature and the urban skyline. Admission for adults is ¥500 (≈ $3), and the garden is typically open from 9:00 AM to 5:30 PM, with last entry at 5:00 PM. It is usually closed on Mondays, or the next day if Monday is a national holiday, so it’s wise to check their official schedule.

In stark contrast to the garden's tranquility, the area is also home to a lively entertainment district that comes alive, especially in the evening. Here, you'll find the impressive Kabukicho Tower, a towering entertainment complex that reaches 225 meters (738 feet) into the sky. This modern building houses a variety of attractions, including restaurants, an arcade, a movie theater, and live music venues. It's a place where you can easily spend several hours enjoying different forms of entertainment.

Nearby, atop the Toho Cinema building, is the prominent Godzilla monument. This large, lifelike replica of the iconic monster’s head appears to peer down at the streets below, making it a popular spot for photos. It’s a fun, quirky landmark that highlights the city's pop culture influence.

Just a short walk from both the tower and the monster monument is Golden Gai, a truly unique collection of tiny bars nestled within narrow alleyways. This area is characterized by its compact buildings, many of which are only big enough to seat five to ten people at a time. Each bar has its own distinct personality, some adorned with quirky decorations, others specializing in particular music genres or drinks. While some bars cater specifically to a regular local clientele, many are welcoming to first-time visitors from overseas. Visitors can experience the intimate atmosphere, chat with locals and other travelers, and observe a slice of the area's nightlife. Be aware that some bars in Golden Gai may have a cover charge, typically ranging from ¥500 (≈ $3) to ¥1,500 (≈ $10), in addition to the cost of drinks. It’s always polite to check for signs or ask about any cover charges before settling in. Locals often have a favorite bar they frequent, while visitors might hop between a few to find one that suits their taste.

For a panoramic view of the entire cityscape, including the areas mentioned above, consider visiting the Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building. Its observation decks, located in both the North and South towers, are open to the public for free. From an elevation of 202 meters (663 feet), you can enjoy expansive views, which are particularly stunning at sunset or after dark.

> **What’s a reasonable budget for a day exploring these attractions?**

Your budget can vary widely depending on your choices. Entry to the National Garden is ¥500 (≈ $3). Visiting the Godzilla monument and the Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building observation decks are free. If you choose to explore Golden Gai, budget for potential cover charges (¥500-¥1,500, or ≈ $3-$10 per bar) and the cost of drinks, which might be ¥800-¥1,500 (≈ $5-$10) per drink. For meals, you can find budget-friendly options starting from around ¥1,000 (≈ $7) per meal at casual eateries, while a meal at a department-store food hall or restaurant in Kabukicho Tower could range from ¥2,000 (≈ $14) to ¥5,000 (≈ $34) or more. For a full day including garden entry, a couple of drinks in Golden Gai, and two meals, a reasonable budget might be around ¥6,000-¥10,000 (≈ $41-$68) per person, not including extensive shopping or very high-end dining. Transportation costs within the city also need to be factored in, usually a few hundred yen per train ride.

> **When is the best time to visit Shinjuku?**

The best time to visit depends on what you want to see. The National Garden is beautiful year-round, but it's especially popular during cherry blossom season (late March to early April) and autumn foliage (late November to early December), though these times also mean larger crowds. For the entertainment district, the atmosphere truly picks up in the late afternoon and evening, with the neon lights of the Kabukicho Tower and Golden Gai creating a vibrant backdrop. Daytime in the entertainment district is generally quieter. To avoid the peak train congestion during rush hour (roughly 7:30 AM – 9:30 AM and 5:00 PM – 7:00 PM), plan your train travel outside these times or be prepared for very crowded conditions.

> **Are these attractions accessible for visitors with mobility challenges?**

The National Garden has relatively flat pathways and accessible routes, and they provide maps indicating these. However, some areas, especially around ponds or more traditional garden sections, might involve steps or uneven surfaces. The Kabukicho Tower and the Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building are modern facilities with elevators and accessible restrooms, making them generally easy to navigate. Golden Gai, on the other hand, consists of very narrow alleys and tiny bars, many of which have steps at their entrances or only offer counter seating, making it challenging for wheelchair users or those with limited mobility. While navigating the alleys is possible, entering many of the individual bars might prove difficult.

> **What if I prefer quiet places over bustling nightlife or large crowds?**

If you prefer a quieter experience, focus your visit on the National Garden during weekdays, especially in the morning when it's less crowded. You can spend several hours leisurely exploring its various sections. For meals, instead of the lively restaurants of the entertainment district, consider the basement food halls of the large department stores. These "food halls" offer an incredible array of pre-made gourmet foods, fresh produce, and baked goods, perfect for assembling a high-quality picnic to enjoy in the garden or taking back to your accommodation. While the food halls themselves can be busy, the atmosphere is different from the nightlife areas. The Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building's observation decks can also offer a peaceful experience, especially during off-peak hours, allowing you to enjoy the views without feeling overwhelmed by crowds.

> **Is the new Tokyu Kabukicho Tower open to children?**

There are no general age restrictions for entering the Tokyu Kabukicho Tower itself. You can freely walk into the main building and access common areas. However, the tower is a large complex housing many different types of establishments, and individual businesses within the tower may have their own specific age restrictions. This is a common practice in entertainment districts, and it means that while you can enter the tower, your access to certain venues inside might be limited depending on the age of your child.

Many of the venues are designed for adult entertainment, such as bars, nightclubs, and some performance spaces, which legally restrict entry to individuals aged 18 or 20 and older, particularly when alcohol is served. Some restaurants might also have policies that discourage or restrict young children, especially during evening hours, even if not legally required. The higher floors, which house hotel lobbies, a cinema, and dining options, are generally more accessible, but it's always wise to check with specific establishments if you plan to visit a particular one with children. For instance, the cinema will admit children for age-appropriate films, but the overall atmosphere of the surrounding district and some areas within the tower itself are distinctly adult-oriented.

> **What kind of activities can children participate in, or at least observe, inside the tower?**

Given the tower's primary focus on adult entertainment and dining, options for children are quite limited. The main activity that children can realistically participate in is watching a movie at the cinema located within the tower. Ticket prices for a standard screening typically start around ¥2,000 (≈ $14) for adults, with children's tickets often slightly less. You can also visit some of the casual dining establishments or cafes, especially during daytime hours, for a meal or a snack. Many of these places offer typical Japanese comfort food and drinks. The various floors also house art installations and digital displays, which can be interesting to observe for a short period. For instance, there's a large video screen that displays dynamic visuals. However, beyond these, there are no dedicated play areas, children's shops, or family-focused entertainment options like amusement rides. Most of the other venues, such as bars, live music clubs, and gaming centers, will either be age-restricted or simply not suitable for children. Locals generally do not bring young children to this area, especially in the evenings, due to its adult-centric nature.

> **What are the typical costs for food and entertainment inside the tower that would be suitable for families?**

Dining costs can vary significantly depending on the type of restaurant. For a casual meal at one of the food court-style areas or a mid-range restaurant, you might expect to pay around ¥1,500 to ¥3,000 (≈ $10 to $20) per person for a main dish and a drink. For example, a bowl of noodles might be around ¥1,000 (≈ $7), while a set meal could be closer to ¥2,500 (≈ $17). Some of the more upscale restaurants on higher floors will naturally have higher prices, easily exceeding ¥5,000 (≈ $34) per person. As mentioned, cinema tickets are typically ¥2,000 (≈ $14) for adults and often around ¥1,000 (≈ $7) for children, depending on age and film type. There are no other common entertainment options for children that involve a direct cost, as most other venues are age-restricted. Therefore, a family of four visiting the cinema and having a casual meal could expect to spend somewhere between ¥8,000 to ¥15,000 (≈ $54 to $101) for a few hours.

> **Are there any risks or concerns for foreign visitors bringing children to this area, especially at night?**

While Japan is generally a very safe country, the Kabukicho area, where the Tokyu Kabukicho Tower is located, is a well-known entertainment district. This means that at night, it becomes very crowded with people going to bars, clubs, and various adult establishments. While the risk of violent crime is low but not zero, the atmosphere can be overwhelming for children and their parents. You might encounter touts attempting to solicit customers for bars, or intoxicated individuals, particularly as the evening progresses. There's also a higher density of smoking in public areas compared to other parts of the city. The tower itself is modern and well-maintained, but exiting into the surrounding streets, especially after 7 or 8 PM, can expose children to sights and sounds that are not typically considered family-friendly. It is generally recommended that families with young children avoid the immediate surrounding streets of Kabukicho late at night. The main tower entrance is usually well-lit and monitored, but the immediate vicinity can be very busy and loud.

> **Are there better family-friendly alternatives nearby if the tower isn't suitable?**

Absolutely. If you are looking for family-friendly entertainment and dining in the wider Shinjuku area, there are several excellent alternatives. Shinjuku Gyoen National Garden, a large park spanning 58.3 hectares (144 acres), offers vast green spaces, beautiful gardens, and walking paths, perfect for an afternoon stroll or picnic. Entry is typically around ¥500 (≈ $3) for adults and free for children under 15. The Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building offers free observation decks on its 45th floor, providing panoramic views of the city from approximately 202 meters (663 feet) high, which children often enjoy. The department stores in Shinjuku, like Isetan or Takashimaya, have extensive food halls and various restaurants that are generally very welcoming to families. They also often feature dedicated children's clothing and toy departments. For more active entertainment, indoor amusement centers with arcade games or bowling alleys, which are widespread across the city, would be far more suitable and enjoyable for children than the Tokyu Kabukicho Tower's primary offerings.

> **Are hot springs with radium in the water safe for use?**

Many natural hot springs contain a variety of dissolved minerals and gases, including trace amounts of naturally occurring radioactive elements like radium. This is a characteristic of some geological formations, and such springs have been used by locals for centuries. While specific scientific proof about their long-term health benefits or risks can be complex and hard to pinpoint precisely, the general sentiment among people here is overwhelmingly positive.

A key point to consider is that Japan is well-known as one of the countries with the longest life expectancies in the world. Many older residents, particularly those living in areas rich with hot springs, use these facilities frequently – often daily, and sometimes even multiple times within a single day. Despite this widespread and long-standing practice, the overall health and longevity of the population remain exceptional. This perspective suggests that concerns about the very low levels of naturally occurring radioactive elements should not be a major deterrent for most visitors. For locals, the experience is largely about comfort and how it makes them feel. If a hot spring experience is relaxing and enjoyable, that is considered the most important factor.

When visiting, you can expect to find a wide range of hot springs, from simple public bathhouses to luxurious resort facilities. A typical day visit to a well-maintained hot spring facility might cost around ¥1,500 (≈ $10) to ¥2,500 (≈ $17), though more elaborate options or overnight stays would naturally be more expensive.

> **What is the typical etiquette visitors should follow when using a hot spring?**

Understanding and following local customs is crucial for a comfortable and respectful experience. First and foremost, you must wash thoroughly before entering the main bathing area. This usually involves sitting on a small stool at a designated washing station, using soap and shampoo to clean your entire body, and rinsing off completely. Once clean, you can enter the hot spring pools. It is customary to enter the water slowly, allowing your body to adjust to the temperature. The water in the hot spring itself is for soaking, not for washing. Do not bring your large towel into the bathing area; instead, use a small hand towel (provided or brought by you) to discreetly cover yourself when moving between pools, or place it on your head or at the side of the pool while soaking. Never let your towel touch the hot spring water. When you exit the pools, dry yourself off as much as possible with your small towel before returning to the changing room, to avoid dripping water everywhere. Most hot springs are gender-segregated, and all bathers are expected to be fully unclothed in the bathing area.

> **Are there any health conditions that might make using hot springs unsafe for some individuals?**

While hot springs are generally considered safe and beneficial for most people, certain health conditions warrant caution or avoidance. The primary concern is the heat, which can be intense. Individuals with high blood pressure, heart conditions, or circulatory problems should consult a medical professional before visiting, as the hot water can significantly affect blood flow and heart rate. Pregnant individuals should also exercise caution or avoid very hot baths, especially during the first trimester. People with open wounds, severe skin conditions, or infectious diseases should refrain from using public hot springs to prevent discomfort for themselves and to maintain hygiene for others. Always stay hydrated, especially in hotter pools, and if you feel dizzy or unwell at any point, exit the water immediately and rest. The risk of fainting or overexertion, though low, is not zero, so it is always wise to listen to your body and avoid staying in the hottest water for too long, especially if you are not accustomed to it.

> **I have tattoos. Can I still visit hot springs?**

Historically, tattoos have been associated with certain groups in Japan, leading many hot springs, especially traditional ones, to prohibit entry for tattooed individuals. However, this policy is gradually changing, particularly in areas frequented by international visitors. Many modern or tourist-oriented facilities are becoming more accommodating. If your tattoos are small, you might be able to cover them discreetly with a waterproof patch (available at many convenience stores or hot spring facilities for a small fee, often around ¥100 to ¥300 (≈ $1 to $2)). For larger or more visible tattoos, your options include seeking out hot springs that explicitly state they are tattoo-friendly (often indicated on their websites or signage), booking a private hot spring bath (called a "family bath" or "private bath"), or staying at a traditional inn that offers hot springs in guest rooms. When in doubt, it is always best to inquire beforehand to avoid disappointment. Some facilities might allow entry if the tattoos are fully covered, while others maintain a strict no-tattoo policy regardless of size or coverage.

> **What are the typical costs associated with an overnight stay at a traditional inn with a hot spring?**

An overnight stay at a traditional inn that includes access to hot springs, often with dinner and breakfast, can vary significantly in price. Generally, you can expect to pay anywhere from ¥15,000 (≈ $101) to ¥50,000 (≈ $338) per person per night. More luxurious or renowned inns, especially those in popular hot spring towns or with spectacular views and elaborate multi-course meals, can exceed ¥70,000 (≈ $473) per person. These prices typically include shared hot spring facilities, and sometimes access to reservable private baths for an additional fee or free of charge for a limited time. It is important to note that rates are often higher on weekends, national holidays, and during peak travel seasons like spring cherry blossom season or autumn foliage season. Many inns offer different room types and meal plans, allowing for some flexibility in your budget. Booking in advance, especially for popular locations or during busy times, is highly recommended to secure your preferred options and potentially better rates.

> **Where can we find K-pop Seventeen merchandise in Tokyo?**
Shin-Okubo is the premier destination for K-pop merchandise and Korean culture in Tokyo. Often called Tokyo's "Korea Town," this vibrant district is where you will find a vast array of goods, including official albums, light sticks, apparel, photo cards, and fan-made items for groups like Seventeen, as well as many other popular K-pop artists. Beyond merchandise, Shin-Okubo also offers an immersive experience with numerous Korean restaurants, cafes, and cosmetic shops.

Shin-Okubo is conveniently located just one stop north of Shinjuku Station on the Yamanote Line, a major loop line in Tokyo. The journey takes less than 2 minutes by train. Alternatively, if you are starting from the east side of Shinjuku Station, it is possible to walk to Shin-Okubo in about 15 to 20 minutes (approximately 1 to 1.5 kilometers or 0.6 to 0.9 miles), depending on your pace and exact starting point in Shinjuku. The main shopping street of Shin-Okubo, Shin-Okubo-dori, is immediately visible upon exiting Shin-Okubo Station.

The shops in Shin-Okubo are typically small to medium-sized, often multi-story, and can be quite crowded, especially on weekends. You will find dedicated K-pop stores that stock official merchandise imported directly from South Korea, alongside smaller independent shops offering a mix of official and unofficial fan-made goods. While many shops primarily sell K-pop items, some also offer a range of Korean beauty products, snacks, and fashion. Most stores accept major credit cards, but it is always wise for visitors to carry some cash, especially for smaller purchases or at independent vendors who might prefer cash. Prices for items vary widely depending on the type of product. A new K-pop album might cost around ¥3,000 (≈ $20), while official light sticks can range from ¥5,000 to ¥7,000 (≈ $34 to $47). Smaller items like photo card sets or keychains might be priced from ¥500 to ¥1,500 (≈ $3 to $10).

Most established stores in Shin-Okubo strive to sell authentic, officially licensed merchandise. However, like in any popular tourist and shopping area, there is a possibility of encountering unofficial or fan-made items. These are generally clearly distinguishable by their branding or packaging and are often sold at lower price points. If purchasing an item like an album, checking for official distributor stickers or holographic seals can help confirm authenticity. For visitors, it is generally safe to assume that products in reputable-looking shops are genuine.

> **How much money should I set aside for K-pop merchandise in Shin-Okubo?**
Your budget will depend entirely on what you wish to purchase. If you are looking for a single official album, expect to pay around ¥3,000 to ¥4,500 (≈ $20 to $30). An official light stick, which is a popular fan item, typically costs ¥5,000 to ¥7,000 (≈ $34 to $47). For t-shirts or hoodies, prices can range from ¥4,000 to ¥8,000 (≈ $27 to $54). Smaller items like keychains, badges, or unofficial photo cards are much more affordable, often in the range of ¥500 to ¥1,500 (≈ $3 to $10) each. If you plan on buying several items, a budget of ¥10,000 to ¥20,000 (≈ $68 to $135) would allow for a good selection, perhaps an album, a light stick, and a few smaller souvenirs. Remember to factor in any food or drink purchases as well, as Shin-Okubo is also a great place to sample Korean cuisine and snacks.

> **When is the best time to visit Shin-Okubo for shopping, to avoid crowds?**
Shin-Okubo is a very popular destination, so it can get crowded, especially on weekends and public holidays. To minimize crowds, the best time for visitors to explore is on a weekday morning, shortly after shops open, which is typically between 10:00 AM and 11:00 AM. Weekday afternoons before 3:00 PM are also generally less busy than evenings or weekends. Saturdays and Sundays, particularly in the afternoon, see a significant increase in visitors, making the streets and shops very packed. If you can only visit on a weekend, arriving right when shops open might offer a slightly less crowded experience for the first hour or two.

> **Are there any other places in Tokyo where I can find K-pop merchandise, or is Shin-Okubo the only option?**
While Shin-Okubo is overwhelmingly the best and most concentrated place for K-pop merchandise, you might find a very limited selection in a few other places. Large electronics retailers like BIC CAMERA or Yodobashi Camera, particularly their larger branches in areas like Shinjuku, Ikebukuro, or Akihabara, sometimes have a small music section that includes a limited range of K-pop albums. column18:
Japan is home to some stunning castles, and here are four of the best that I highly recommend visiting.

First, Himeji Castle – This is the king of Japanese castles. Its white exterior and grand structure make it one of the most famous and well-preserved castles in the country. Himeji Castle is a UNESCO World Heritage site, and walking through its grounds feels like stepping back in time. It’s impressive from every angle.

Next is Hirosaki Castle in Aomori. Hirosaki isn’t just about the castle – the surrounding town has kept its old, historic atmosphere. Visiting during cherry blossom season is especially beautiful, as the castle park is filled with sakura trees. The blend of the old town and the castle creates a magical experience.

Shurijo Castle in Okinawa offers a different experience. This castle isn’t your typical samurai fortress – it represents the Ryukyu Kingdom’s history. The architecture, colors, and layout feel distinct from mainland castles. It’s massive, and you can feel the cultural richness of Okinawa as you explore the site.

Lastly, Takeda Castle – also known as "Japan’s Machu Picchu." This castle is in ruins, but the views from the top of the mountain are absolutely breathtaking. On foggy mornings, the castle appears to float above the clouds. It’s one of those places you have to see to believe.

column2: Name of place where noodles are dropped onto bamboo tubes for diners?
column3:
That fun and unique summer dining experience is called 流しそうめん (nagashi sōmen) in Japanese!

🍜 What is it?
Thin wheat noodles (sōmen) are sent flowing down a stream of cold water in a bamboo flume.

Diners catch the noodles with chopsticks as they pass by, then dip them into a light soy-based sauce before eating.

It's a traditional and playful way to enjoy noodles, especially popular in the summer.

📍 Famous Places to Try It:
Here are a few well-known spots in Japan where you can experience nagashi sōmen:

1. Hirobun (ひろ文) – Kibune, Kyoto
The most iconic spot in Japan for nagashi sōmen!

Set in the mountains of Kibune, the bamboo flumes run over a river — stunning in summer.

🌿 Usually open from May to September.

Very popular → advance reservation or early arrival recommended.

2. Tōsenkyo Sōmen Nagashi (唐船峡そうめん流し) – Kagoshima
Located in Ibusuki, it's more of a circular "spinning" style with a stream of cold water, very family-friendly.

Open year-round thanks to warm climate.

column2: Tips for first timers in Japan: Get the limousine bus, Suica, and Shinkansen tickets in advance.
column14:
We’ve been back from Japan a couple of weeks and here are some of my tips for first timers:
First up .... Be prepared to arrive back home and want to go back straight away!! 
Get the limousine bus!!! If your hotel is near to a limo bus stop get the bus! It was so easy and stress-less. There’s a big ticket counter for Narita Airport Buses. The staff speak English and the bus stop was just a 2 minute walk away and clearly signposted. If your bus ticket says it leaves at 6pm, it leaves at 6pm. That’s your bus!!! They tag your bags (up to two pieces of luggage each) and put them under the bus. It’s very quick and efficient. Yes, the train is probably 30 minutes faster but I was tired after a 10 hour flight so finding train platforms and navigating stations with luggage was the last thing I wanted to do. 
With Shinkansen tickets, we tried to buy them the day before if we were near a station. Usually we’d know our schedule for the next day so it was easier to have our tickets in hand rather than having to go early and stand in line for tickets. I wasn’t sure of the ticket machines so preferred to speak to a person at a manned office. I’d screenshot the train and time I wanted and showed them that on my phone so nothing go lost in translation. We had one trip where we didn’t buy our ticket as we didn’t know what time we were leaving Nagano back to Tokyo. It happened to be the end of a holiday weekend and there were no reserved seats. No big deal as we found seats in the non-reserved car but a couple of stops further along people were standing in the aisles of the train so I guess if you’re traveling during busy seasons it may be a good idea to pre-purchase tickets even if it’s just a day or two in advance. 
Luggage on Shinkansen ... check my photo on how to store some luggage if you're traveling in a group. The chairs turn so you're facing each other which makes space behind your chair for luggage storage. I wouldn't recommend doing this if you're facing strangers as the legroom becomes a lot less. Totally fine if you're with friends or family. Otherwise there's space above you for luggage. My husband lifted our big black one onto the shelf above us for a couple of our journeys. Just make sure it's on the shelf safely and won't fall on anyone!
SUICA!! If you have an iPhone get the Suica! It made our lives SO much easier. Tap in and tap out on trains and you’re done. We used them to pay for things at stores and also on the bus in Kyoto. No standing in line for tickets. You can add money as you go. Any remaining balance, use at a combini. It’s especially useful if traveling in a group otherwise if half of you have a Suica and the other half don’t then you’re still waiting for those standing in line for tickets!
Airalo - we each got a 10GB SIM card and we used it constantly over about 13 days. We used it in Tokyo, Kyoto and a random little far flung place called Omaezaki (where we had an event to go to) and it worked perfectly everywhere. We probably used about 6GB max in that time. 
The weather … check it online and think about how you personally react to weather. A couple of people had said in various groups that it was warmer before we left. When we got there it was cold (for me). There were days where it was too hot for a puffer jacket and days where it was very cold and wet. Weather can be changeable so don’t rely on personal opinions. Check the forecast online. It's usually pretty accurate. If you're unsure take layers. 
Be prepared to walk! We were going to take it easy on our first day as I wasn’t feeling too well but we ended up doing over 22,000 steps! Also, be ok with your itinerary changing. Everything takes longer than you expect. Walking in crowds, finding the right platform in the station, stopping to take photos, queuing for food, etc, takes time so just go with the flow! We averaged about 22-25,000 a day!! And in all honesty, I didn’t feel tired by the end of it. There was so much to see, do, eat, that I didn’t want to stop! 
We did Tsujiki and Senso-ji on a Saturday 🤪 It was SO BUSY and it wasn’t even peak season. It wasn’t just tourists but locals too. Go as early as you can to places you know will be extra busy…. Or later in the day. Having said that there really is no avoiding the mass of people. There are queues are everywhere! Be prepared to wait to buy food at some places and sometimes the wait is worth it. At Tsujiki we saw a long line and had no idea what it was for but we passed the stall and it smelled so damn good that we stood in line for an hour. It was the best beef stew ever!! 
Tokyo felt completely safe wherever we went. In fact, all of Japan. I mention Tokyo specifically as it’s a big city. The only time we had anyone approach us was a homeless man near Kabuchiko but we didn’t feel unsafe. He asked for money and left. 
It’s impeccably clean. Even public restrooms! Please keep it that way. Take your trash home with you or find a trash can (if you get lucky enough to find one!). Sometimes if you've just bought food from a vendor and you eat it nearby they'll take the trash and dispose of it for you.
The never-ending subject of leggings!!! 🤣 I wore leggings … Just not the see-through, butt-crack showing leggings! People are so busy and in a rush to get where they need to be that no one will care what you’re wearing. There is a vast range of fashion and dress style in Japan which I LOVED. So many incredible, unique, eccentric styles pulled off so perfectly. I genuinely don’t think anyone is going to bat an eyelid at your leggings unless they really are the see-through kind! My friend was wearing hers often. She’s an athlete and has no need to cover up with anything baggy and no one gave her any sideways glances. And yes, there are some people that wear sweatpants here… big baggy sweats are actually in fashion at the moment. So wear the athleisure if you want to but just dress it up a tad!
So much hype about the combinis! Fun place to see but I found it to be a lot of not so healthy food wrapped in a lot of plastic. That's my personal opinion. I did write about this in a comment somewhere. Got a few angry faces which is fine because each to their own. Having said that the convenience stores are convenient! Eg, grabbing a hot water and being able to make my own tea on the go, or finding hand warmers in a 7/11 at 10pm or the onigiri which was the only food I really had any urge to buy at a combinis. FYI, did you know that the onigiri from combinis have numbers on them and you follow the numbers to open the wrapper?! We didn’t know until a friend told us. Pull down on no1, and pull out on 2 & 3 and voila you have a perfectly wrapped onigiri! Also, can I just add… if you aren't in a rush and don't have to buy from a combini, support small local businesses as much as possible 🙂 Coming from a small island, I know how important this is for smaller businesses to survive. The best onigiri we had was street food in Kyoto. We grabbed onigiri from the 7/11 when we were rushing to catch a train. 
Google translate, Google lens (and Google maps) will be your best friends. The Japanese are so gracious and do their best to help and understand us but not everyone speaks English and, those that do, don’t speak it perfectly. I read something which will always stick with me : “Never make fun of someone who speaks broken English. It means they know another language.” If they can make an effort to speak a foreign language we can make the effort to learn a few key phrases before we go. Even if it’s just saying thank you or excuse me. In my humble opinion, being polite and kind takes you a long way. And more importantly it paves the way for the next visitors who come along. Please don’t ruin it for the next generation. So many countries have rude tourists which have turned the locals into begrudging hosts. Having lived on two islands which need tourism to survive I have experienced this first hand.
I chose our first and last hotels on the basis of there being a limousine bus stop outside the hotel to make our trip to and from the airport easier. I really struggled with sleeping due to the hard beds! After a long day you want a comfy bed and out of 4 hotels we stayed out only one had a comfortable bed. The rooms are mostly small but that was totally ok with us as we just used the room to sleep & shower. In all honesty, we could have spent a lot less on our hotel rooms as we barely spent any time in them. If you’re a couple, here’s a tip - Get a twin room rather than a double. They’re usually more spacious. I ended up with a bad back and trapped nerves in my neck and arms by the end of the trip. I was so happy to get back to my bed! 
Travel light! It’ll make life a lot easier for yourself! I packed one suitcase for two of us and a foldable bag for any purchases I made while there. Talking of purchases, don’t leave your shopping to the last day like I did!! 🙃 I barely bought anything because I was too busy sight-seeing and by the last day I was so overwhelmed with the huge scale of shops and not knowing where to go that I barely did any shopping. I found that the department stores were extraordinarily big and not as enjoyable as shopping in smaller local shops. I enjoyed buying a knife in a small shop in Kappabashi and speaking to the owner about different knives. I also enjoyed finding a little boutique clothes shop near Kappabashi. I got to meet the designer of some of the clothes in the store and bought some insane wide pants (which I’m still not sure I can pull off). He was so sweet and he gifted me a tote bag. We found a little gem of a family run sushi place in Shinjuku called Ko Sushi. We went there twice on our last two nights. Each night they gifted us some nigiri and on leaving gave us some rice crackers. The second night the little old lady and her son stood outside the restaurant and wave us off. We found people to be kind and generous and the more of an effort you make the more they return the sentiment.
Google maps … I could not have survived without it! It worked near perfectly. The only issue we had was that the platform for the Shinkansen was not always correct so make sure to check the info boards or your ticket for which platform you’re leaving from. Otherwise for all other trains it was spot on. I loved how it told you which train car to sit in so you get out and you’re as near to your exit as possible. 
Follow the arrows!! Some stations have you walking on one side and then suddenly you’re on the other. Most of them are all the same but a couple of them in Tokyo were a law unto themselves!
Food … almost all the food we had was outstanding. We wanted to try so many new things and we did. The only bad food we had was when we hadn’t done any research and were so hungry we just stopped off somewhere without checking reviews and it was my least favorite food. Not bad, just not great. I know everyone says you’ll find somewhere to eat as you but I prefer to do my research and read reviews!
Ichiran vs Tatsunoya … Ichiran is a cool experience with the little single booth seating, you receive your bowl of ramen via a little hole in front of you and get a bow from the server after he passes it to you. Despite the unique experience, the ramen itself wasn’t even in my top 3 ramen at all! Tatsunoya in Shinjuku won hands down. We went there twice and stood in a long line twice but it was SO worth it! Here’s how it works at Tatsunoya : Get in line, eventually the server will call you in to order from a machine, get the tickets, stand outside, he comes back and takes half your tickets and you wait in line until it’s your turn. 
Finally do your research! I lived and breathed Japan before we went! I had YouTube videos playing every spare moment I had! I did so much Googling and read through countless posts in FB groups and if I couldn’t find an answer I’d ask a question and people would so graciously give me an answer. If your question is generic, do a group search first 😉 All my research really paid off as I was well prepared for everything - public transport, food, etiquette, places to see, etc … except shopping which I didn’t realise would be so overwhelming! 🤣

There are two ways to get a card. You can buy a "Welcome SUICA" at the airport, or you can use your smartphone by downloading "Mobile SUICA" or "Mobile PASMO." If you’re using a smartphone, you can easily set it up with Apple Pay or Google Pay. Super convenient, and no need to carry a physical card!

column2: Lots of tax free shops when you spend over 5,500 yen. How do we get reimbursed?
column3:
​In Japan, many stores offer a tax-free shopping benefit to foreign visitors, allowing you to save the 10% consumption tax on eligible purchases. Here's how you can take advantage of this:​

Who: Non-residents staying in Japan for less than six months.​
Wikipedia

What: Purchases totaling at least ¥5,000 (excluding tax) in a single day at a single store. Consumable items have a maximum purchase limit of ¥500,000 to qualify. ​
2. Identifying Tax-Free Stores:

Look for stores displaying the "Japan Tax-Free Shop" logo. These establishments participate in the tax-free program. ​

3. Making Tax-Free Purchases:

At the Time of Purchase:

Inform the Staff: Let the cashier know you wish to make a tax-free purchase.​

Present Your Passport: The original passport with your entry stamp is required; copies are not accepted. ​

Payment: Pay the price excluding the consumption tax.​

At a Tax-Free Counter:

In some cases, you may need to pay the full price first and then proceed to a designated tax-free counter within the store to process your refund. This must be done on the same day of purchase. ​

4. Important Considerations:

Consumable Items: Items like food, cosmetics, and beverages will be sealed in a special bag, which must not be opened until you leave Japan. ​

Combining Purchases: General items and consumables cannot be combined to meet the minimum purchase amount; each category must individually meet the ¥5,000 threshold. ​

Same-Day Processing: Tax-free procedures must be completed on the same day of purchase at the store where you bought the items. ​

5. Departure Procedures:

Customs Declaration: Be prepared to present your tax-free items and receipts to customs officials when departing Japan. Ensure that consumable items remain sealed. ​

By following these steps, you can enjoy tax-free shopping in Japan and make the most of your purchases.

column2: 日本でしか食べれない、高級な食材って何？
column3:
🐟 1. 本マグロ（特に大間産）
青森・大間の本マグロは初競りで数千万円になるほど。

脂のノリ・身のしまり・味のバランスが極上。

海外でもマグロはあるけど、このレベルは日本の漁と保存・流通技術があるからこそ。

🐄 2. 和牛（特に神戸牛・松阪牛・近江牛）
A5ランクの霜降り肉、独特の甘みと柔らかさ。

海外でも"wagyu"として人気だけど、本物の認定和牛は日本国内のみに限定されてるものも多い。

飼育法、血統管理、マッサージなど、職人レベルでの管理。

🍈 3. 夕張メロン
北海道・夕張でしか栽培されない、完熟メロンの王様。

贈答用は1玉2万〜5万円、初競りは数百万円に。

糖度・香り・果肉のやわらかさが他と別格。

🍷 4. 黒トリュフ × 国産卵（"たまごかけご飯"として）
実は日本の卵の品質は世界一とも言われていて、生で安心して食べられるのはほぼ日本だけ。

海外の人から見れば「TKG（たまごかけごはん）」も高級グルメに。

トリュフを贅沢に削る「トリュフ卵かけごはん」は都内の高級店でも提供。

🦀 5. 越前ガニ（福井）、松葉ガニ（鳥取）、香箱ガニ（石川）などのタグ付きズワイガニ
一杯数万円〜十数万円。タグ付きは漁場・品質保証の証。

鮮度・身入り・甘みが超一級。

特定期間・地域でしか水揚げされないため、超限定。

🍵 6. 宇治抹茶（特に手摘み一番茶）
京都・宇治で栽培された「覆い下栽培」の高級抹茶。

一番茶（春に摘む最高級）になると、ほんの数十グラムで数千円〜。

海外の抹茶とは風味の深さとまろやかさが段違い。

🍄 7. 松茸（国産）
秋の風物詩。人工栽培が難しく、天然ものが主。

国産（特に長野・岩手など）は海外産（中国・カナダ産）と比べて香りが濃厚。

🚅 If you miss your reserved Shinkansen:
If you bought a reserved seat ticket and miss your train, you can still use the same ticket on the next train, but only in the non-reserved seating cars, on the same day.

If you're very late and miss the day entirely, the ticket becomes invalid unless the fare portion is refundable (depends on where/how you bought it).

✅ So yes — you can still ride later that day, just not in the reserved seat section.

🧾 Best websites to book Shinkansen in advance:

SmartEX (JR Central & JR West)

Covers Tokaido, Sanyo, and Kyushu Shinkansen (Tokyo ⇄ Osaka ⇄ Hiroshima ⇄ Fukuoka).

English available, and you can use IC cards (like Suica) as your ticket.

JR East Train Reservation

Great for Tokyo ⇄ Nagano, Sendai, Aomori, etc.

You can pick up tickets at vending machines or stations.

Klook or Japan Experience

User-friendly for international tourists.

Sometimes includes special deals or easier cancellation.

column17:
If you want a local and peaceful side of Tokyo, Sumida City is a great pick! This area offers a more traditional and relaxed experience, perfect for families with young children. You'll enjoy visiting the iconic Tokyo Skytree, which not only provides breathtaking views but also has the Solamachi mall with child-friendly stores and dining options. 1. Karuizawa (Nagano Prefecture)
🌨️ A chic mountain town that often gets snow in winter.

Ice skating, outlet shopping, and cozy cafés.

Snowy trees and European-style townscapes = very photogenic!

📍 Access:

🚅 1 hour from Tokyo by Hokuriku Shinkansen

2. Gala Yuzawa (Niigata Prefecture)
🎿 The most convenient ski resort from Tokyo.

Directly connected to the Shinkansen station.

Even if you don’t ski, you can enjoy snow play, cable cars, and scenic views.

📍 Access:

🚅 About 75 min from Tokyo on the Joetsu Shinkansen

3. Nikko (Tochigi Prefecture)
🏯 When it snows, Nikko’s shrines and bridges look magical.

Not guaranteed snow, but if timing is right (esp. Jan–Feb), it’s stunning.

Combine culture + nature in one trip.

📍 Access:

🚃 Around 2 hours from Tokyo via Tobu Railway

4. Minakami (Gunma Prefecture)
❄️ Snowy rivers, hot springs, and peaceful countryside vibes.

Good spot for snowshoeing or just soaking in an open-air onsen with snowy views.

📍 Access:

🚅 About 70–90 minutes from Tokyo via Joetsu Shinkansen + local train

1. Kinosaki Onsen (Hyogo Prefecture)
(Best with 1 night but doable as a long day trip)

📍 Access:

🚅 About 2.5 hours from Osaka via Limited Express "Kounotori"

🏯 If you catch a snowy day, this lakeside castle is breathtaking with snow on the roof and gardens.

Lake Biwa nearby adds to the beauty.

🚃 About 1.5 hours from Osaka by JR

❄️ Snow-covered shrines in the mountains north of Kyoto.

The red lanterns and torii gates against the white snow are iconic.

Great for a peaceful snowy walk.

📍 Access:

🚃 Around 1.5 hours from Osaka via train to Kyoto + Eizan Railway

✨ Must-See Winter Festivals & Illuminations Near Tokyo
1. Chichibu Night Festival (Saitama)
When: December 2nd–3rd (every year)

Why it’s special: A UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage event with massive floats, taiko drums, traditional music, and a fireworks show against the winter sky

Vibe: Like Gion Matsuri, but in winter!

Access: About 90 minutes from Tokyo by train (Seibu Line to Chichibu Station)

Tip: Arrive early, dress warm, and prepare for crowds

2. Sagamiko Illumillion (Kanagawa)
When: Early November – Early May

Why it’s special: Over 6 million LED lights cover the mountainside at Sagamiko Resort Pleasure Forest

Best for: Couples, families, and photo-lovers

Access: About 1 hour from Tokyo by train (JR Chuo Line to Sagamiko Station + bus)

Tip: Go on a weekday evening for fewer crowds

3. Tokyo Dome City Winter Illumination
When: Late November – Late February

Why it’s special: Free entry, interactive light displays, and fun atmosphere for families and couples

Location: Central Tokyo – easy to drop by after shopping or sightseeing

Access: Right next to Suidobashi Station

Tip: Great for visitors with limited time who want something magical without leaving the city

4. Roppongi Hills Christmas Illumination
When: Early November – December 25th

Why it’s special: Elegant white-and-blue lights along Keyakizaka Street with views of Tokyo Tower

Bonus: Nearby Christmas market adds to the cozy European vibe

Access: Roppongi Station, central Tokyo

Tip: Take photos around sunset for best lighting

5. Ashikaga Flower Park “Flower Fantasy” (Tochigi)
When: Mid-October – Mid-February

Why it’s special: Over 5 million lights arranged into flower-shaped and seasonal designs

One of Japan’s top-rated illuminations

Access: About 2 hours from Tokyo (JR Ueno Station → Oyama → Ashikaga Flower Park Station)

Tip: Perfect for a romantic day + night trip

Extra Travel Tips
Wear warm clothes: These events are mostly outdoors and can get very cold at night

Bring a tripod or phone stand for beautiful light-up photos

Check event websites for the latest times and any weather updates

Try local street food—many events have special food stalls

column2: Do hotels and ryokans in Japan offer allergy-friendly or vegan meals?
column3:
🏨 Hotels in Japan
✅ Large Hotels (especially in major cities and tourist areas)
Often offer vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free, or allergy-friendly meal options on request.

Buffets may label allergens (egg, dairy, wheat, etc.).

International chains (e.g., Hilton, Marriott, Hyatt) are usually more accommodating.

📌 Tip: Always inform the hotel at the time of booking, and follow up a few days before arrival. Japanese hospitality is excellent, but they appreciate notice!

🏯 Ryokans (Traditional Japanese Inns)
✅ Upscale Ryokans (like Hoshinoya, Gora Kadan, etc.)
Can customize kaiseki meals for allergies and vegetarian/vegan diets.

Some even have fully plant-based menus or halal-friendly options.

Many use fresh, local ingredients — which can be adapted easily if given notice.

❗ Small, family-run ryokans
May have limited ability to adjust traditional dishes, especially if fish broth (dashi) is used.

Vegan = more difficult unless you communicate very clearly and in advance.

🧾 Key Phrases to Use (in Japanese or written form)
私はヴィーガンです（I’m vegan）

動物性の食材（肉、魚、卵、乳製品など）は食べられません。
(I cannot eat animal-based ingredients: meat, fish, eggs, dairy, etc.)

〇〇アレルギーがあります（I have an allergy to __）
Example: 小麦アレルギー (wheat allergy), 卵アレルギー (egg allergy)

🥗 Bonus: Japan-wide Vegan-Friendly Hotel Chains or Spots
Hotel Metropolitan (Tokyo, Nagano, etc.) – some branches offer vegetarian menus.

Onsen ryokans in Kyoto or Kinosaki – many now have vegan options upon request.

Shukubo (temple lodgings) – especially in Koyasan or Mt. Haguro, serve shojin ryori (Buddhist vegan cuisine).

⛔️ Many close reception around 9:00–10:00 PM, and late check-in is not always allowed.
🕰️ If you plan to arrive late, you must contact them in advance. Some may not accept check-in after hours at all.

Early morning check-out (e.g., 5 AM):
✅ Usually no problem. Just settle your bill the night before or use self check-out (available at many hotels).

Late check-out (after official time, usually 10–11 AM):
⛔️ Not usually free.
💴 You can often pay for extended stay (1–2 hours), but not always guaranteed.
📞 Ask at the front desk in advance — late check-out is by request and not common in Japan.

🧳 Pro Tip:
Many hotels offer free luggage storage before check-in and after check-out.

If your flight or train is very early/late, airport hotels or hotels near major stations (like Tokyo or Shin-Osaka) are ideal.

🧍‍♂️✨ Tattoos in Japan: Social Perception
In Japan, tattoos are still sometimes associated with organized crime (yakuza) — especially large, traditional-style body art.

But! Attitudes are slowly changing, especially among younger people and in big cities.

Tourists with tattoos are common now, and most people won’t react negatively, especially in places like Tokyo, Osaka, or Kyoto.

💦 Places Where Tattoos Might Be an Issue
Location	Are Tattoos Allowed?	What to Do?
Onsen / Public Baths	❌ Often not allowed	✅ Book a private onsen (貸切風呂) or cover tattoos with patches
Swimming Pools / Gyms	🟡 Some ban visible tattoos	✅ Wear a rash guard or ask at the front desk
Ryokan (traditional inns)	🟡 Depends on the place	✅ Ask in advance, or choose tattoo-friendly ones
Beaches / Public areas	✅ Generally okay	Just be respectful and avoid flashing full-body ink in super rural areas

column21:
Planning a night out in Tokyo and wondering what to wear? 👀 If you're a guy hitting the clubs, here's what you need to know to avoid getting turned away at the door.

🕺 It Depends on the Club
In Japan, club dress codes vary from place to place. Some are pretty chill, but others can be strict—especially in major cities like Tokyo and Osaka.

At big-name venues like WOMB, V2 Tokyo, or Odeon, the rules may be more relaxed for foreigners. That said, even these places will judge you based on your overall appearance.

🚫 What Not to Wear
A few common no-gos:

Shorts

Sandals

Tank tops

Even in the summer, many clubs won’t let men in wearing super casual outfits. You don’t need a suit, but smart casual goes a long way.

✅ What to Wear Instead
Aim for something like this:

Nice jeans or pants

Clean sneakers or shoes (not flip-flops!)

A fitted shirt or stylish tee

A jacket or blazer if it’s cool out

Basically, dress like you're going to impress—but not like you're headed to a job interview.

🎟️ Don’t Lose Your Wristband
Many clubs use wristbands or hand stamps to track who’s paid entry. If you leave the club and want to come back in, you’ll need to show it—so don’t peel it off or wash it off too soon.

💡 Pro Tip
Even if you’re a tourist, being well-dressed makes it way easier to get in and vibe with the crowd. Japanese clubs care about atmosphere and image, so blend in with confidence.

About Earthquake prediction..Anyone aware of this ? I am leaving next week to Tokyo and this came out …:
column3:
1. Earthquakes happen often — but serious damage is rare
Japan experiences frequent small earthquakes due to its location, but most are harmless.

Thanks to strict building codes, modern construction, and emergency planning, it’s very rare for people to die from earthquakes — especially in places where most travelers stay (like hotels and newer buildings in cities).

While old wooden homes (古民家) might be vulnerable, hotels, apartments, and public buildings in Tokyo are built to withstand strong shaking.

🌊 2. What to watch out for: Tsunami & fires
In coastal areas, tsunami risk exists after a large quake. That’s why you should:

Move to higher ground if near the sea and you feel a long or strong quake

Always follow official alerts or hotel staff instructions

Fires can also break out due to gas leaks after a quake — stay alert and evacuate calmly if necessary.

🔔 3. Japan has an early warning system
Your phone will automatically receive an alert (even with foreign SIMs) when a strong quake is approaching.

You can also download apps like:

Safety Tips (by Japan Tourism)

Yurekuru Call

Earthquake Network

🧘‍♂️ 4. Stay calm & prepared
Don’t let earthquake anxiety ruin your trip — Japanese people live with this risk every day and go about life normally.

Learn where emergency exits are at your hotel

If a quake hits:

Stay indoors and duck under a table

Avoid windows and shelves

Do not run outside during shaking

✋ In short:
💡 Most earthquakes in Japan are safe to live through, especially for travelers in cities.
🧳 Just be informed, stay calm, and enjoy your trip!
